text:
LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents : https://t.co/vIW9CIY7FN

"Qingni Wang†SimularChangdae OhUniversity of Wisconsin–MadisonYuzhe Yang†SimularSharon LiUniversity of Wisconsin–MadisonJiachen YangSimularAng LiSimularXin Eric WangSimular
Abstract
Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor. To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent’s latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward. LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model’s hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty. During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training. Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55–11.94 points at matched escalation rates. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.
Figure 1:Accuracy–cost comparison between LEASH and random task-level routing on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The area spanned by random routing is obtained from repeated random task allocations across different escalation budgets; the band shows ±1 standard deviation over 10,000 allocations. At matched inference cost, LEASH achieves 9.1 percentage points higher task success.
1Introduction
Computer-use agents (CUAs) automate tasks of graphical interfaces by translating natural-language instructions and visual observations into executable actions (Xie et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024), and are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon automation tasks that can take more than an hour on average (Abhyankar et al., 2026). While frontier proprietary models have been shown to achieve impressive performance leaps (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026a), running every single task spanning hundreds of steps with these models raises cost concerns, whereas a light open-weight model alone performs poorly on even much simpler tasks (Xie et al., 2024). This creates a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and cost efficiency, motivating weak-to-strong escalation (W2SE), in which a weak agent serves as the primary executor and hands control to a strong agent only when needed (Wei et al., 2026; Lei and Huang, 2026). W2SE raises two important questions: (1) When should the weak agent escalate, and (2) who oversees the strong agent after handing over?Existing work on W2SE primarily focuses on the first question, estimating the weak agent’s failure risk to decide when escalation is needed. Some of them adopt another monitoring agent to verify each step (Wang et al., 2024; Yi et al., 2026), others train an extra monitoring module on the collection of annotated trajectories (Wei et al., 2026; Lei and Huang, 2026). However, the former inevitably adds nontrivial cost to run another heavy agent step-by-step, whereas the latter creates another phase of data annotation and training, hindering direct adoption in real-world applications under varying deployment constraints. While training-free uncertainty estimation-based approaches might avoid the aforementioned bottlenecks (Oh et al., 2026b), prior works still rely on external knowledge base (Liu et al., 2026), another reference model (Oh et al., 2026a), or multiple sampling for each step (Wang et al., 2026) quickly becomes infeasible or impractical in long-horizon tasks in the wild.Besides, escalation alone does not eliminate execution uncertainty, resulting in the second important question in W2SE which is commonly overlooked. That is, even after a stronger agent takes control, subsequent actions may deviate from the intended task or fail to achieve the desired outcome. However, monitoring a black-box strong agent is challenging because its internal states are inaccessible and verbalized confidence can be unreliable on evolving context of long-horizon task (Han et al., 2024; Kirchhof et al., 2026).To answer both questions, we formulate W2SE as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, and use the weak agent’s failure risk as a proxy for the expected benefit of escalation. We then propose Latent uncertainty for Escalation And SHadow oversight (LEASH), a training-free framework driven by the uncertainty signal in the weak agent’s hidden states. First, we record its hidden states of prompt and action tokens on a small set of held-out tasks and label them with task-level and subgoal-level outcomes to construct a representation bank. This representation bank then serves as a semantic anchor to score the newly faced prompts and actions during test-time by measuring, under a Mahalanobis metric in latent space, how much closer each one lies to past failures than to past successes. LEASH puts this signal on two jobs (Figure 2): For escalation, an initial gate scores uncertainty from the task prompt query, while a runtime gate monitors subsequent execution trace. For oversight, after the weak model hands the control to the strong agent, it switches its role from actor to observer that monitors the strong agent’s trajectory every three steps; when its uncertainty is high, the pending action is rolled back and re-decided once with higher reasoning effort. Importantly, our uncertainty-driven W2SE formulation draws on an easily accessible resource, the weak agent’s own past experience (Silver and Sutton, 2025), removing reliance on an external dataset or additional training without hosting another expensive agent during runtime, while offering extensibility for recursive self-improvement (Schmidhuber, 2007; Zelikman et al., 2022; Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023).We evaluate LEASH on OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) with four open-weight weak agents and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b) as the strong agent. At matched escalation rates, LEASH outperforms random escalation by 6.55–11.94 points. We further measure how much of the performance gap between the weak agent alone and always-on Opus is recovered by escalation, following the performance-gap metric of (Burns et al., 2023). LEASH recovers 75–102% of this gap, against 37–69% for random escalation, while costing 69–81% as much as always-on Opus. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), LEASH matches always-on Opus (73.7% vs. 72.9% success) at 19% lower cost, whereas random escalation at equal cost scores about 9 points lower (Figure 1).📷Figure 2:Overview of uncertainty-aware weak-to-strong escalation and post-handoff oversight. A weak agent goes through the task until its uncertainty scores trigger initial or step-level escalation; otherwise, the weak agent continues. After escalation is triggered, the strong agent retains control while the weak agent changes its role from an actor to a shadow observer for continued monitoring. The feedback path from weak observer to strong actor enables uncertainty-triggered reflection and intervention. In short, LEASH unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent’s latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•We formalize weak-to-strong escalation as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem and show that one latent uncertainty signal can drive both escalation and oversight.
•We propose a training-free, scalable uncertainty scoring method that measures how much closer a hidden state lies to the weak agent’s own past failures than to its past successes, and provide theoretical justification for using this score for escalation.
•We extend this uncertainty signal to weak-to-strong oversight, in which the white-box weak agent monitors the black-box strong agent through its own hidden states.
•On OSWorld with four open-weight backbones, we show that LEASH outperforms random escalation at matched escalation rates and recovers 75–102% of the escalation gap at 69–81% of the cost of using always strong agent.
2Related Work

Efficient Computer-Use Agents.
Model routing and cascading offer a promising way to balance inference cost and performance, as demonstrated by FrugalGPT and RouteLLM (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2025; Dekoninck et al., 2025). Extending this idea to GUI automation, Adaptive VLM Routing selects models based on action difficulty and confidence (Liu et al., 2026), while StepWise trains lightweight monitors to detect execution stalls and identify milestones for escalation (Wei et al., 2026). Our work instead leverages the backbone agent’s internal representations to guide both task-level routing and step-level escalation, without training a dedicated monitoring network.
Weak-to-Strong Paradigms.
Weak-to-strong generalization studies how stronger models learn from weaker supervision (Burns et al., 2023; Somerstep et al., 2025; Medvedev et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025). These works primarily concern training-time transfer of supervision or capabilities from a weaker model to a stronger one. Here we study the complementary inference-time setting of weak-to-strong escalation (W2SE), where a weak model executes by default and selectively invokes a stronger model when additional capability is needed. This shifts the weak–strong relationship from supervision transfer to sequential resource allocation. We derive escalation signals from the agent’s own past experience without training an additional monitor.
Uncertainty Estimation and Agent Monitoring.
Uncertainty estimation of agentic systems has emerged as one of the most important problems to monitor and guide agent decisions (Oh et al., 2026b; Chun et al., 2026; Han et al., 2024), while SafeGround and Argus investigate uncertainty estimation for GUI grounding, including calibrated predictions and representation-based methods (Wang et al., 2026; Kumar et al., 2026). Sampling-based uncertainty estimation and risk control have also been studied for question answering (Duan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), but repeated generation can be costly when applied at every step of a long-horizon agent trajectory. Meanwhile, another line of work explores weak-to-strong oversight of agent misbehavior and failure monitoring through observable trajectories (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Kale et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Rather than focusing on either escalation or oversight alone, we handle both problem in a single unified fueled by a simple uncertainty estimate. That is, we integrate representation-based uncertainty estimation into the execution workflow, reusing the backbone model’s hidden states for escalation and extending the same signal to post-handoff oversight of a closed-source strong agent.
3Method
We introduce LEASH, a training-free uncertainty-driven agentic inference framework for W2SE and post-handoff oversight (Figure 2). By comparing the weak model’s runtime hidden states with successful and failed reference executions, we estimate uncertainty at task initialization and during execution, which guides both escalation to the strong agent and continued oversight after handoff. We first formulate the problem in Section 3.1 and introduce each component in subsequent sections.
3.1Problem Formulation
Given a task query, a computer-use agent generates an action conditioned on the query, the screen, and history. We consider a lightweight, weak agent, e.g., a relatively small open-weight model with accessible hidden states, and a large, strong agent, e.g., a proprietary black-box frontier model, sharing a budget of T actions. In addition to these two actor agents, we also host a Manager agent (with a strong model) who fires at the beginning to decompose the task and subsequently at subgoal boundaries to verify progress, constructing a minimal version of multi-agent workflow (Agashe et al., 2025a; Agashe et al., 2025b; Koh et al., 2026). Throughout execution, the Manager decomposes the task query into subgoals with screenshot-verifiable completion criteria and decides whether to advance, keep, or revise each subgoal (Appendix C). This decomposition naturally provides finer-grained supervision (Chun and Russakovsky, 2026), allowing execution steps to inherit subgoal-level outcomes rather than relying solely on the final task-level label.maxπ⁡𝔼x∼𝒟​[Sπ​(x)]s.t.Prx∼𝒟⁡(tescπ​(x)<T)≤pesc,(1)We adopt the weak model as a starting agent for all tasks until control is transferred to the strong model by hitting some flags. Then, the strong model runs over the remaining action budget until the end of the task. Let x∼𝒟 denote a task drawn from the task distribution, and let π denote an escalation policy. For each task x, policy π induces a stopping time tescπ​(x)∈{0,1,…,T}, where tescπ​(x)=0 denotes the earliest escalation opportunity and tescπ​(x)=T denotes no escalation. Since the strong agent dominates per-step cost, we use the total escalation rate, pesc, as a budget proxy and want to maximize task success under limited budget:📷Figure 3:Construction of the query and action reference banks for latent space uncertainty estimation.
where Sπ​(x)∈{0,1} indicates task success under escalation policy π. That is, we want to run tasks and each step within them through the weak agent as many times as possible unless it fails, to minimize the cost while achieving a high task success rate, becoming a problem when-to-escalate. Unlike existing works that adopt other monitoring agents (Wang et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026) incurring additional inference costs or training-based monitors (Wei et al., 2026) requiring annotation costs and an additional training phase, we propose to use simple uncertainty estimates as a signal to determine when-to-escalate, without inducing any training cost.
3.2Reference-Based Latent Uncertainty Estimation
Motivated by well-established observations revealing that LLMs internalize the likelihood of task success or failure in their representations (Kadavath et al., 2022; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Kossen et al., 2024; Orgad et al., 2025) even before generating any tokens (Ji et al., 2024; Cencerrado et al., 2025; Afzal et al., 2025), we propose a training-free, representation-distance-based uncertainty estimation technique for agent systems.
Representations and reference banks.
For each task from a small held-out set, we run a weak agent to collect some preliminary inference trajectories without escalating anything to a strong agent. During this inference over the held-out set, we extract two final-layer representations, h0∈ℝd at the last task query prompt token, and ht∈ℝd at the last generated action token of each execution step t. The former captures information over the instruction and initial screen before decoding, whereas the latter also incorporates the action executed by the agent. These hidden states build representation banks pairing each hidden state with progress outcome: The query bank ℬq={(hi,0,yi)} adopts task outcomes yi∈{Pass,Fail}, whereas the action bank ℬa={(hi,t,yi,t)} assigns each step its corresponding subgoal segment’s outcome (assessed by a Manager agent): Pass if the subgoal is successfully completed, Fail if it should be revised, and otherwise the final task outcome.
Uncertainty score.
For each channel of representation banks c∈{q,a}, i.e., query and action, we fit a shared-covariance Gaussian discriminant model (Mukhoti et al., 2023) on ℬc. We first standardize each representation with the bank statistics, zc​(h)=(h−h¯c)/sc, where h¯c,sc∈ℝd are the feature-wise mean and standard deviation of all hidden states in ℬc (pooled over both outcomes) and the division is element-wise. Let μc,y be the centroid of the standardized representations in ℬc with outcome y, and Σc,λ=Σ^c+λc​I the pooled within-class covariance regularized by λc>0. Using the squared Mahalanobis distance,dc,y2​(h)=(zc​(h)−μc,y)⊤​Σc,λ−1​(zc​(h)−μc,y),(2)we define uncertainty score through the relative distance to successful and failed references:uc​(h)=dc,Pass2​(h)−dc,Fail2​(h).(3)A larger score indicates greater relative proximity to failed references. We use uq for initialization and ua for runtime action monitoring, selecting λc for each model backbone and channel by task-grouped cross-validated AUROC (detailed in Appendix A.2).
Interpretation.
The design of our score was largely motivated by distance-based out-of-distribution detection literature (Lee et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2023; Müller and Hein, 2025), but with careful customization for better fit in step-level agent uncertainty estimation. Unlike the relative Mahalanobis distance of Ren et al. (2021), which subtracts a class-agnostic background distance, we subtract the distance to the opposite outcome to capture a sharp delta signal of failure. Note that the Gaussian fitting only requires per-outcome means and a singular value decomposition, without gradient-based training, and can be iterated as the bank grows through multiple rounds of experience (Shinn et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026).
3.3Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation

Escalation gates.
With the measure of uncertainty, we define escalation gates for each uncertainty channel. Two channels address different sources of uncertainty: ambiguity in task specification and failure likelihood across stacked interactions (Oh et al., 2026b). The initial query-level routing can identify tasks beyond the weak agent’s capability in advance, but cannot anticipate every difficulty encountered during runtime execution. Therefore, we combine an initial escalation gate, g0=𝕀{uq(h0)>τq} which routes when g0=1, with a runtime escalation gate, gt=𝕀{ua(ht)>τa} for t≥1 that monitors each action of tasks retained by the initial gate given calibrated thresholds τq and τa. Runtime escalation occurs immediately after the first action with gt=1; The strong agent then receives the instruction, current screenshot, and recent steps run by the weak agent, and keeps control until the task termination (See Appendix C for details).
Calibrating gating threshold to an escalation budget.
We set each threshold to a quantile of uncertainty scores on the reference tasks, so that each gate escalates a target fraction of tasks used to construct the representation bank. Let pq be the target fraction of tasks escalated at initialization and pesc the target overall escalation rate. Since the runtime gate only monitors the tasks that the initial gate leaves to the weak agent, it should escalate a fraction pa=(pesc−pq)/(1−pq) of them, so that pq+(1−pq)​pa=pesc. The thresholds are then expressed as follows:τq=Q1−pq​({uq​(hi,0)}i),τa=Q1−pa​({Ui:uq​(hi,0)≤τq}),(4)where Qα is the empirical α-quantile over reference tasks and Ui=max1≤t≤Ti⁡ua​(hi,t) is the maximum runtime score of the i-th reference trajectory of length Ti. Intuitively, a fraction pq of the reference tasks have initial scores above τq, and among the tasks kept by the initial gate, a fraction pa have a maximum runtime score above τa. Note that we target escalation rates rather than failure probabilities because the gates only use the ranking of the scores. We compute τa from each task’s maximum score because a single step above τa is enough for handoff; a quantile over individual steps would typically escalate more tasks than targeted. All scores in Eq. (4) are obtained out-of-fold from the same held-out reference set. After the thresholds are fixed, we refit one final estimator per uncertainty channel on all tasks in this same reference set for evaluation. Because refitting slightly changes the score scale, the target escalation rates are only approximate; we therefore report realized rates and match random baselines to them (Table 1, Appendix A.3).
3.4Post-Handoff Oversight and Intervention
We note that the strong agent can also get stuck in repeated action loops or get lost in multi-turn interactions (Laban et al., 2026). However, its hidden states are inaccessible, while verbalized confidence is often highly unreliable as an uncertainty signal (Han et al., 2024; Kirchhof et al., 2026).
Shadow oversight.
To handle this challenge, we repurpose the weak agent from an actor as a Shadow observer of strong agent for continued post-handoff oversight. We append each executed strong-agent step to the weak model’s history in its own action format and query with the current observation every k steps (k=3 by default). Given that context, the weak model generates a candidate action, allowing us to extract shadow representation htsh at the same action token position as the strong black-box agent. Assuming that a higher uncertainty from the weak model also indicates a greater difficulty for the strong agent on average (Pan et al., 2026; Kale et al., 2026), we can use that representation for the runtime action uncertainty estimation again ush=ua​(htsh), to define the Shadow oversight gate gsh=𝕀{ush>τsh} given a threshold τsh.
Uncertainty-triggered intervention.
When gsh=1, we discard the strong agent’s pending action and trigger a reflection-based intervention, which prompts the strong model agent to reassess its own progress toward the task goal and choose a new action using higher reasoning effort. We set the threshold τsh to the 90th percentile of per-step reference scores of the action representation bank. We allow at most six Shadow interventions per task (Vasudev et al., 2026) and terminate further intervention once two have altered the strong agent’s proposed action (Appendix A.4).
4Experiments

4.1Experimental Setup

Benchmark and agents.
We evaluate our framework on OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024). For the weak agent, we use four open-source model backbones: EvoCUA-8B (Xue et al., 2026), Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni (30B-A3B) (Deshmukh et al., 2026), and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b). For the strong agent that takes over the escalated task and the Manager agent that decomposes tasks into subgoals and verifies their completion, we use Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b). We compare our uncertainty-based W2SE and oversight framework and the baseline against always-on Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025), which use those models for every task and every step. More detailed definitions, execution settings, and model identifiers are provided in Appendix B.1.
Metrics.
We report task success rate and mean inference cost per task. Costs are estimated from recorded token usage at fixed reference prices, including weak agent, Manager, strong-executor, and monitoring calls when enabled. These estimates measure the token-priced inference cost of the overall workflow. Cost coverage and accounting details are provided in Appendix B.1.

text:
Meta says it has fixed an issue following reports that its smart glasses recorded conversations without anyone saying “Hey Meta”.

One Ray-Ban Meta owner reported finding audio recordings and transcripts of ordinary conversations in the Meta AI app across three pairs of glasses. They said the setting allowing responses without the wake phrase was switched off.

Android Authority obtained Meta’s response, but says it has not independently reproduced the behaviour. How many devices were affected, what caused it and what happened to unintentionally captured audio remain unanswered in the reporting.

Smart glasses have useful applications. They also put microphones into conversations involving people who never bought the product, opened the app or agreed to its settings.

Meta points owners towards controls for reviewing and deleting voice logs. That offers little reassurance to the person standing opposite them.

Fixing the issue matters. Explaining it matters too. People deserve to know how an ordinary conversation became a saved recording, and what safeguards now prevent it happening again.

Nobody actually wants a website.

They want booked calls, inbound leads, and revenue.

The moment your proposal focuses on deliverables like : 

• A 5-page responsive site.
• Custom animations.
• Clean layouts and modern typography.

...you are actively turning yourself into a commodity competing on price.

A dentist never wakes up thinking:
"Man, I really need better typography on my site."

They wake up thinking:
"Why did 300 people visit our page this week and nobody booked an appointment?"

When you pitch, shift the entire frame:
Identify the single action the client actually needs visitors to take.

Position your entire offer around fixing the bottleneck stopping that action.
Present your design by showing how each section guides a visitor to take that step.

Clients don't pay premium rates for Figma files, page counts, or code.

They pay for the business result the website produces.
Sell the outcome, not the asset.

text:
EliteReplay: Preserving Diverse Solutions in RL Post-Training via Quality-Diversity Search : https://t.co/bpCxmez3H8

"Hanane Nour MoussaDoeun LeeSachin KumarThe Ohio State University{moussa.45, lee.11501, kumar.1145}@osu.edu
Abstract
Reinforcement learning has become a common post-training technique to improve the accuracy of LLMs on verifiable tasks. However, such training can narrow the set of solutions the model can produce. Several approaches have attempted to address this behavior-sharpening effect, but they often optimize metrics that do not reflect the diversity of correct solutions. Ideally, we want a model that can produce multiple good solutions, not only a single reliable one. We propose EliteReplay, a post-training recipe that pairs GRPO with an “elite” archive built by quality-diversity search. Before training, we use the frozen base model to collect solutions that span distinct approaches; during training, GRPO is combined with a replay loss on this archive. The result is a post-trained model that improves accuracy while preserving more of the base model’s solution diversity. On multiple text-to-SQL tasks, EliteReplay achieves the highest pass@128 than all baselines, producing up to 77% more distinct correct strategies than the strongest baselines. It preserves most of the base model’s correct strategies, outperforming existing methods in strategy retention. This diversity translates into practical benefits on ambiguous questions, where EliteReplay covers both interpretations nearly twice as often as the strongest baseline on AmbiQT11All artifacts can be found at https://t.co/oUytXJkvPD.
1Introduction
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard post-training technique for large language model (LLM) reasoning (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). However, studies show that common RLVR methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improve performance via sharpening, i.e. concentrating probability on a few behaviors the base model already had (Yue et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025). RL post-training therefore improves reliability (pass@1), but often by reducing reach (pass@k) (Oh et al., 2026).Figure 1:Accuracy versus strategy diversity at k=128. Each point is a post-trained model on BIRD (in-distribution) and Spider (out-of-distribution). EliteReplay reaches the highest pass@128 while producing far more distinct correct strategies.
Several works seek to recover this lost reach by improving pass@k relative to the base model (Tajwar et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Walder and Karkhanis, 2025). Since recovering reach may require retaining alternative ways of solving problems, pass@k has also become a common proxy for diversity (Dang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Yu, 2025; Jiang et al., 2026). Yet pass@k only asks whether some sample is correct, not whether the correct samples differ. A model can therefore achieve high pass@k by reliably producing a single strategy for each question while losing the alternatives the base model once exhibited.Retaining these alternative ways of solving a problem, its solution diversity, is important whenever the approach matters alongside the final answer. Different correct solutions may follow distinct reasoning paths, differ in computational efficiency, or encode different interpretations of an ambiguous request. Systems that rely on repeated sampling and selection also benefit from having meaningful variety (Li et al., 2022; Pourreza et al., 2025). As Figure 1 shows, methods with nearly identical pass@128 can differ substantially in the number of distinct correct strategies they produce.Preserving a diverse set of good solutions is the central concern of quality-diversity (QD) optimization. Rather than seeking a single optimum, QD algorithms such as novelty search (Lehman and Stanley, 2011) and MAP-Elites (Mouret and Clune, 2015) maintain an archive of high-performing solutions spread across a space of behavior descriptors. In the deep RL literature, such archives have been coupled with policy-gradient learners to broaden exploration, enabling the discovery of new behaviors in policies trained from scratch (Khadka and Tumer, 2018; Pourchot and Sigaud, 2019; Ecoffet et al., 2021). Post-training a language model, however, presents a different challenge, since the base model already exhibits a variety of correct strategies that RL can suppress. At the same time, language models offer a natural advantage for QD search, as the base model itself can propose meaningful variations through repeated sampling (Lehman et al., 2023; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Bradley et al., 2024; Samvelyan et al., 2024).We study whether quality-diversity archives can preserve solution diversity during GRPO training. Our method, EliteReplay, first runs MAP-Elites with the frozen base model to build an elite archive: a set of verified solutions, with at most one solution per cell of a grid indexed by a behavior descriptor. It then trains with GRPO while adding a small replay loss on this archive.Measuring diversity requires distinguishing how solutions are obtained, not just whether they are correct. We therefore evaluate diversity at the level of solution strategies, using a structural description of how each solution solves the question, computed deterministically from the solution itself. This allows us to measure U@k, the number of unique correct strategies among k samples, alongside effective diversity (Shypula et al., 2025), the probability that two random samples are both correct and different, which captures improvements in reliability without sacrificing diversity.We evaluate EliteReplay on text-to-SQL, a natural testbed where questions can admit multiple correct queries and natural-language ambiguity is common. As shown in Figure 1, EliteReplay achieves 74.8% pass@128 on BIRD (Li et al., 2023), comparable to MaxRL’s 73.7%, while producing 9.1 distinct correct strategies per question compared to just 6.2. On the out-of-distribution Spider (Yu et al., 2018), it achieves 93.2% pass@128, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.3 percentage points while producing up to 77% more distinct correct strategies. EliteReplay also retains 62% and 60% of the base model’s correct strategies on BIRD and Spider, respectively, at least 23 percentage points more than any baseline. This preserved diversity also benefits ambiguous questions, with EliteReplay covering both interpretations on 27.0% of AmbiQT (Bhaskar et al., 2023) questions, compared to 14.2% for the strongest baseline.Our contributions are:
•We propose EliteReplay, which anchors RL to an elite archive constructed through quality-diversity search using the base model (§2).
•We evaluate RL post-training through strategy-level diversity, measuring unique correct strategies (U@k), effective diversity, and retention of the base model’s strategies (§3).
•We show that EliteReplay preserves more diverse correct strategies while maintaining strong pass@k, retains most base-model strategies, and better covers ambiguous questions (§5).Figure 2:Overview of EliteReplay. (a) Before training, MAP-Elites with the frozen base model builds a per-question elite archive, keeping one verified solution per behavior cell. (b) During training, GRPO is combined with a replay loss on the fixed archive. The figure illustrates the method on text-to-SQL.

2EliteReplay
Our proposed approach improves accuracy with RL while preserving the base model’s distinct correct solutions in two stages (Figure 2). Before training, QD search with the frozen base model builds an elite archive of verified solutions that span distinct approaches (§2.1). During training, GRPO is combined with a replay loss on this archive (§2.2). Appendix A details both stages.
2.1Constructing the elite archive
RL post-training tends to concentrate probability on a narrower set of approaches (Yue et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025), putting alternative correct approaches at risk of disappearing. Simply replaying solutions sampled from the base model may not prevent this collapse, since such samples are dominated by the base model’s more frequent approaches and underrepresent rarer ones. We therefore build the replay set using quality-diversity search (Pugh et al., 2016), instantiating MAP-Elites (Mouret and Clune, 2015), a QD algorithm that partitions a space of behavior descriptors into cells and retains the best solution found in each, on a subset 𝒟A of the training questions, using the frozen base model π0 to generate candidate solutions. For each question x∈𝒟A, we maintain an archive 𝒜x of verified solutions, organized into cells by solution approach. Each cell stores at most one solution, or elite, allowing the archive to represent multiple correct approaches to the same question.
Defining the behavior space.
Classical MAP-Elites relies on behavior descriptors designed by hand for each domain. Instead, we first collect a set of verified seed solutions from the base model and provide them to a separate LLM, the labeler, as representative examples of how the task can be solved. Using these examples, the labeler induces a broader vocabulary of possible approaches, including ones not observed in the seeds, to guide subsequent exploration. The labeler assigns each solution an approach label, capturing its general method of solving the question. To distinguish solutions that follow the same broad approach but differ in their structure, we combine this label with structural features extracted deterministically from the solution (e.g., joins or subqueries in SQL, loops or recursion in code). The resulting behavior descriptor b⁡(y) determines the solution’s archive cell. This descriptor is used only to guide search; we evaluate diversity with a separate, deterministic notion of strategy (§3). Appendix A.2 details the behavior space, and Appendices B.1 and B.2 give the features and labeler prompts used in our text-to-SQL experiments.
Constructing the archive.
Given this behavior space, we populate and expand the per-question archives through four steps.
(1)Initialization. We insert the verified seed solutions into their corresponding archive cells, establishing the initial set of elites for each question.
(2)Selection. We choose a target approach among those the labeler judges applicable to the question, prioritizing approaches not yet represented in the archive while balancing attempts across targets (Appendix A.3). We then select a parent elite, preferably one following a different approach.
(3)Variation. We prompt π0 with the original question, target approach, and parent elite, asking it to generate a new solution following the target approach.
(4)Evaluation and insertion. We verify the candidate and, if correct, assign it to the cell corresponding to its actual approach, which may differ from the requested one. The candidate fills an empty cell or replaces an existing elite if it is shorter.We repeat selection, variation, and evaluation for a fixed search budget. Because selection favors untried approaches, search is directed toward approaches that may be correct but rarely sampled by the base model, while candidates repeating an existing approach only compete for an occupied cell. Search more than doubles the cells occupied by seed sampling and yields more distinct elites than direct sampling (Appendices C.1 and C.2). The surviving elites, paired with their original task prompts, form the replay set.
2.2Training with elite replay
Starting from the base model π0, we train the policy πθ with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), while encouraging it to reproduce solutions from the archive. GRPO improves correctness, and archive replay helps preserve alternative approaches.
Replaying archived solutions.
ℒreplay(θ)=−1|ℰ|∑(x,y)∈ℰ1|y|logπθ(y∣x).(1)At each training step, we sample a batch ℰ of verified solutions from the archive, balancing sampling across questions and their occupied cells so that questions with more elites do not dominate. To retain these solutions, we define the replay loss as the negative log-likelihood of the archived solutions, normalized by solution length so that longer solutions do not receive more weight,
Combining replay with GRPO.
Inspired by CHORD (Zhang et al., 2026), we combine the on-policy GRPO objective with the supervised replay loss using a simplified formulation with a fixed mixing weight μℒ⁡(θ)=(1−μ)​ℒGRPO​(θ)+μ​ℒreplay​(θ).(2)The archive remains fixed, and the replay loss provides a consistent signal for preserving alternative solutions alongside GRPO updates (Appendix A.4). At inference, the trained policy is sampled directly, without archive lookup or search.
3Evaluating Strategy Diversity
We measure how well RL post-training preserves the range of correct solutions at the level of solution strategies, using three complementary metrics that capture the number of distinct correct strategies, the structural diversity of correct samples, and the retention of strategies from the base model.
Strategies.
We represent each solution y by a strategy s⁡(y), a deterministic description of how the solution is constructed that abstracts away surface details. For solutions with formal structure, such as code, abstract syntax trees (ASTs) provide a natural basis for distinguishing programs by their structure rather than their surface form (Ren et al., 2020; Song et al., 2024; Shypula et al., 2025). We therefore derive s⁡(y) from the AST of each SQL query, distinguishing, for example, a query that joins two tables from one that filters through a nested subquery (Appendix B.5).
Unique correct strategies (U@k).
Let r⁡(x,y)∈{0,1} indicate whether solution y to question x is correct, and let y1,…,yn be n samples for x. U@k is the expected number of distinct strategies among the correct samples in a random subset of k samples. If cs of the n samples are correct with strategy s, then, analogous to the unbiased pass@k estimator (Chen et al., 2021),U​@​k​(x)=∑s[ 1−(n−csk)/(nk)],(3)averaged over questions. Unlike pass@k, which counts whether at least one correct solution is found, U@k counts how many different correct strategies are represented. The two coincide when all correct samples for a question share a single strategy, while U@k increases as additional correct strategies are found.Figure 3:Pass@k and U@k as the sampling budget grows on BIRD and Spider. EliteReplay improves accuracy relative to the base model while producing far more distinct correct strategies than any baseline.

Effective diversity.
Effective diversity (Shypula et al., 2025) captures how structurally different correct samples are from one another, measuring the expected dissimilarity between two random samples while counting only pairs in which both are correct,ED⁡(x)=2n⁡(n−1)​∑i<jri​rj​(1−sim⁡(yi,yj)),(4)averaged over questions, where ri=r⁡(x,yi) and sim∈[0,1] is an AST-based similarity. By accounting for both correctness and structural differences, effective diversity rewards models that produce correct solutions reliably without collapsing onto similar outputs.
Strategy retention.
Ret⁡(m)=1|𝒬|​∑x∈𝒬|𝒮m​(x)∩𝒮π0​(x)||𝒮π0​(x)|.(5)Let 𝒮m​(x) be the set of strategies that model m produces correctly among its n samples for x, and let 𝒬 be the questions on which the base model π0 produces at least two distinct correct strategies. Retention measures the fraction of these base-model strategies that remain accessible after post-training,
4Experimental Setup

Model and data.
We use Qwen3.5-4B-Base (Qwen Team, 2026) as our base model and train on 5,000 questions from BIRD (Li et al., 2023), a text-to-SQL dataset built from real-world databases. We construct the elite archive using a subset of 1,000 of these questions, which remain part of the RL training pool (Appendix B.1). For evaluation, we use BIRD dev to measure in-distribution performance and Spider 1.0 dev (Yu et al., 2018) to assess out-of-distribution generalization on databases disjoint from those used in training. On both benchmarks, correctness is measured by execution accuracy, comparing the results of generated SQL queries with those of the gold queries on their respective databases (Appendix B.4).To examine the post-training effects in an unrelated domain, we also evaluate on MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021). Finally, to assess the practical value of preserving diverse solutions, we evaluate on AmbiQT (Bhaskar et al., 2023), a benchmark derived from Spider where each question admits two valid interpretations due to ambiguity (e.g. in column or table names, join paths, etc). We draw n=128 samples per question.
Baselines.
We compare EliteReplay against standard GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and three methods aimed at preserving diversity or improving pass@k. MaxRL (Tajwar et al., 2026) upweights hard questions through a maximum-likelihood objective, while DPH-F (Li et al., 2026b) uses forward-KL regularization to preserve the base model’s behavior on questions it already solves reliably. SetPO (Li et al., 2026a) encourages diversity by adding to each rollout’s advantage a bonus for how much it increases the semantic diversity of its sampled group. All methods are trained on the same data for 100 steps, with EliteReplay using a replay weight of μ=0.05 (Appendix C.3). Appendix B.3 gives further implementation and compute details.
5Results and Analysis

5.1Accuracy and strategy diversity
Figure 4:MATH-500 pass@k of BIRD-trained models. Baselines barely improve or degrade relative to the base model, whereas EliteReplay substantially improves it, despite not being trained on math.
Figure 5:Effective diversity, the probability (%) that two samples are both correct and structurally different. EliteReplay scores highest on both benchmarks.
Figure 6:Share of the base model’s correct strategies retained by each method, over questions on which the base model uses at least two strategies. EliteReplay has the highest retention rate.

EliteReplay improves reliability while substantially preserving diversity.
All post-trained methods improve pass@1 on BIRD, raising it from 25.3% for the base model to 52–56%. However, most lose reach as the sampling budget increases (Figure 3), as observed for RLVR on math (Yue et al., 2025). GRPO, SetPO, and DPH-F attain only 68–69% pass@128, below the base model’s 73.6%, whereas MaxRL and EliteReplay maintain comparable coverage at 73.7% and 74.8%, respectively. On out-of-distribution Spider, EliteReplay achieves the highest pass@k among post-trained methods at every budget, reaching 78.6% pass@1 and 93.2% pass@128, versus at most 76.2% and 86.9% for the baselines.
EliteReplay also maintains performance outside the training domain.
On MATH-500 (Figure 4) three baselines perform worse than the base model across all sampling budgets, with pass@1 falling to 25–27% from 28.3%. In contrast, EliteReplay improves pass@1 to 35.5% while remaining within one point of the base model at large sampling budgets. These results suggest that replay may act as a rehearsal mechanism that mitigates out-of-domain forgetting, which is an interesting area of analysis for future work.
Similar pass@k can conceal substantial differences in strategy diversity.
Despite achieving nearly identical pass@128 on BIRD, EliteReplay produces almost 50% more distinct correct strategies than MaxRL, with U@128 of 9.1 versus 6.2 (Figure 3, right). Thus, MaxRL recovers coverage while relying on fewer ways of solving each question, a distinction that pass@k does not capture. The diversity gap is even larger on Spider, where EliteReplay produces nearly 80% more distinct correct strategies than the strongest baseline (9.4 versus 5.3). On BIRD, EliteReplay also matches or exceeds the base model’s U@k up to k=64, despite substantially higher pass@1, while all baselines fall increasingly behind it at larger budgets.Effective diversity provides complementary evidence (Figure 5). EliteReplay achieves the highest scores on both benchmarks, reaching 25.9% on BIRD versus 23.4% for the strongest baseline. On Spider, it is the only post-training method to exceed the base model (31.4% versus 27.9%).
5.2Preserving base-model strategies

EliteReplay retains substantially more of the base model’s correct strategies.
U@k counts distinct strategies, whereas strategy retention tracks which of the base model’s strategies survive post-training. As shown in Figure 6, the baselines retain only 34–39% of these strategies on BIRD and 30–37% on Spider, whereas EliteReplay retains 62% and 60%, respectively.
EliteReplay preserves broader coverage across individual strategies.
To examine whether the lost strategies are concentrated in a few approaches or spread across many, we measure how often each of the base model’s most common correct strategies are still produced across questions, relative to its original coverage (Appendix Figure 9; details in Appendix B.6). The baselines lose coverage on nearly every strategy, with reductions of up to 28 percentage points on BIRD. In contrast, EliteReplay shows smaller reductions on every strategy, never exceeding 9 percentage points. The same pattern holds on Spider (Appendix C.4).
The baselines often collapse onto a single strategy, while EliteReplay preserves alternatives.
To examine how strategy loss manifests at the question level, we compare the distribution of correct samples across strategies for three representative BIRD questions (Figure 7; details in Appendix B.8). While the baselines often concentrate nearly all correct samples on a single approach, EliteReplay maintains multiple strategies closer to the base model’s original distribution. Notably, the baselines sometimes converge on an approach that the base model rarely used, showing that strategy collapse does not necessarily preserve the base model’s preferred behavior, as Zhao et al. (2025) also observe for RL on math. Spider examples and representative queries for each strategy are provided in Appendices C.5 and C.6.📷Figure 7:How correct samples split across strategies on three BIRD questions. Each row shows the percentage of a method’s correct samples (out of 128 rollouts) that use each strategy. The baselines concentrate on one strategy, while EliteReplay keeps several.

5.3Diversity under ambiguity

Preserved diversity improves coverage of ambiguous questions.
Ambiguous questions provide a practical test of solution diversity, since covering multiple interpretations requires producing distinct correct solutions. For example, “employees of a department” could mean current employees or everyone ever assigned to it. A model that produces only one interpretation cannot cover both, however reliably it generates that answer. On AmbiQT, we report Both@k, the fraction of questions for which k samples match the gold execution result of each interpretation (Table 1; Appendix B.7).k248163264128Base model2.35.510.316.323.030.137.0GRPO1.62.02.43.03.53.94.2SetPO2.55.05.56.77.88.810.0DPH-F2.44.15.97.69.310.812.0MaxRL1.93.76.08.510.812.714.2EliteReplay3.05.99.513.517.922.527.0Table 1:Both@k on AmbiQT (%), the share of questions for which k samples include correct queries for both valid readings. EliteReplay covers both readings most often among post-trained models.
At k=128, GRPO covers both interpretations on only 4.2% of questions, while the strongest diversity-preserving baseline reaches 14.2%. EliteReplay nearly doubles this coverage, achieving 27.0%, with its advantage growing as the sampling budget increases. This improvement closes more than half the gap between the strongest baseline and the base model, which achieves 37.0%.
5.4Ablating archive construction and replay
We isolate the contributions of archive construction and replay through three comparisons, using as a control an independently and identically distributed (IID) archive of verified base-model samples at equal generation budget (Appendix C.2).Figure 8:SFT on the archive alone. $IONQ We have followed IonQ's hiring all year. Name by name.

A lot of these hires came from cyber. People from Zero Trust companies like Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks and Netskope. People who worked cyber for the NSA, the DoD and the Space Force. Security vendor veterans. Cryptography specialists.

We mapped 116 of them:

23 in cryptography, PQC and quantum-safe
22 from security software vendors
20 DevSecOps and cyber engineers at Seed Innovations
14 from government and military cyber
9 from Zero Trust vendors
28 in enterprise security roles

Seed was underestimated. IonQ closed it on January 30. Seed runs a $39M Air Force DevSecOps pipeline and won a $67.8M DoD DevSecOps award.

ID Quantique brings QKD, quantum random numbers and post-quantum cryptography. It already runs national quantum-safe networks in South Korea, Romania, Slovakia and Poland. Its Clarion KX platform combines QKD and PQC key exchange. It runs in Singtel's national network in Singapore. South Korea's NIS certified it for national security. ID Quantique also works with Cisco and Fortinet.

On October 12 IonQ announced it will acquire Elisity. Zero Trust microsegmentation, more than 100 deployments. Close expected in Q4 2026. The shared roadmap will add cryptographic inventory and risk data to Elisity's IdentityGraph. Customers can then prioritize their PQC upgrades by business risk.

So this week's deal was not a surprise.

The calendar explains it. From January 2027, new national security systems must support NSA's CNSA 2.0 algorithms. Federal high-value systems must move key exchange to PQC by 2030 and signatures by 2031. Contractors face the same 2030 date. Every plan starts with a crypto inventory.

IonQ already offers that first step. At its September Investor Day it presented QSPM, quantum security posture management. It shows customers where their infrastructure is vulnerable to quantum attacks.

The pieces line up with how a PQC migration actually works. Inventory and posture with QSPM and the Elisity roadmap. Protect the links with ID Quantique. Enforce Zero Trust with Elisity. Deliver with defense depth through Seed.

The OMB memo goes further. It calls PQC "a foundational dependency" of Zero Trust. Keys and Zero Trust now come as one requirement. IonQ hired for both and bought both.

The contracts are coming. $8.18M with Congruity360 for QKD and PQC. A statewide quantum-safe network with Florida LambdaRail. A Zero Trust framework for quantum computers with ARLIS, sponsored by the Air Force. A place in the MDA SHIELD pool.

Our read on what sets IonQ apart: few quantum players hold both sides. Enterprise reach through Elisity's customers. Defense depth through Seed, a Trusted Foundry at SkyWater and people from the NSA and the DoD.

Growing and integrating all of this takes capital and discipline. IonQ listed 223 open jobs with SkyWater in early October. This week it raised about $2 billion.

I think we will see more and more security contracts.

The map is based on public profiles and is surely incomplete.

Phoenix, AZ — Hunter Biden was seen entering the Arizona Capitol Executive Tower on Thursday as state employees streamed out of it, minutes after the building was evacuated over an envelope of white powder.

The envelope arrived Thursday afternoon at the Arizona Department of State, where staff opened it. The office called police and hazmat responders, isolated the material and the people who had been exposed, evacuated everyone else and shut off access to the floor. The tower houses the offices of Gov. Katie Hobbs and Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, who called it a targeted threat. No injuries were reported. The FBI and the Arizona Department of Public Safety are investigating, and the substance has not been identified.

How Biden got there is less clear. The first news alert to mention white powder went out at 3:12 p.m. Biden was photographed walking against the flow of evacuees at 3:19, a timeline that would have required him to travel from Malibu to downtown Phoenix in roughly seven minutes. Aviation experts said no aircraft in existence can do that. Asked about it, Biden said, "You'd be surprised."

"Everybody was running out and he was the only one going in," said a state employee who was evacuated from the fifth floor. "He looked like a firefighter, if a firefighter had just read a headline and couldn't stand it."

Stopped at the stairs by a DPS officer, Biden explained that he was there to help identify the substance, and that he had more relevant field experience than anyone on the hazmat team, which no one present was in a position to dispute. A technician in a full protective suit said Biden then offered to perform what he called a "field test" and was escorted back to the sidewalk.

Biden, who spent much of last month as the country's leading informal expert on gas-station kratom, said he had followed the story the moment he saw the words. "They said 'white powder,'" he told reporters. "What was I supposed to do, not come?"

Asked whether he was worried about legal exposure, he again cited what he called "a pretty good document" covering 2014 through 2024, then looked at his phone, noted that it was October 2026, and conceded that this was something of a gap.

Fontes, who described the envelope as a sobering reminder of the threats facing election workers, said his office would not be scared out of doing its job. Biden said he understood completely, and that he would not be scared out of his.

At press time Biden had been found in a stairwell asking a hazmat officer whether the envelope had a return address, and if so, whether the sender ships to California.

3D Response: Why Must We Wait Until Children Are Murdered Before School Safety Becomes a Priority?

By 3D Response

Our children deserve more than promises after tragedy. They deserve action before the next headline, before the next press conference, and before another family receives the phone call that changes their lives forever.

How many more children must die before those responsible for protecting them decide that school safety deserves the urgency it demands?

It is a question that should haunt every politician, every school superintendent, every state school safety official, every federal agency responsible for protecting our communities, and the President of the United States.

When a tragedy occurs inside a school, the response is tragically predictable. The nation watches in horror. Families grieve. Communities demand answers. Politicians step before cameras, offer condolences, promise investigations, and assure the public that lessons will be learned.

Suddenly, everyone wants to know what went wrong.

Suddenly, school safety becomes a national conversation.

Suddenly, meetings are scheduled, experts are consulted, and officials begin asking questions that should have been asked long before innocent children lost their lives.

But then the headlines fade.

The cameras leave.

The public moves on to the next crisis.

And too often, the urgency disappears with them.

A week later, where is the conversation? Where is the transparency? Where is the follow-through? Where is the accountability?

Most importantly, where is the action?

The Questions Nobody Should Be Afraid to Ask

If politicians have the authority to create laws, allocate funding, and demand accountability, why does it so often take a school tragedy to force them into action?

If superintendents are responsible for overseeing school systems, what are they doing every day to evaluate vulnerabilities, address concerns, and ensure that safety plans are more than documents sitting in an office?

If state school safety officials are tasked with helping schools prepare for threats, what measurable steps are being taken to identify weaknesses before they become fatal?

If federal agencies possess intelligence, investigative resources, and expertise that can help prevent violence, how are those resources being coordinated with schools and local authorities?

And if the President of the United States can bring the nation together after a tragedy, why can’t that same leadership be used to establish a sustained, serious commitment to preventing the next one?

These are not partisan questions. They are questions of responsibility.

Protecting children should never be reduced to a political talking point, an election-year promise, or a debate that resurfaces only when another school becomes a crime scene.

Children do not belong to one political party. Their safety should not depend on which party controls a state, Congress, or the White House.

Why Does Prevention Take a Back Seat to Reaction?

We know that no safety system can eliminate every possible threat. We also know that prevention requires preparation, communication, training, resources, and the willingness to confront uncomfortable realities.

Yet too often, our national response appears to prioritize investigating a tragedy after it happens rather than continually examining what could be done to prevent one.

Why must parents watch their children walk into school with the fear that they might not come home?

Why must teachers practice emergency drills while families wonder whether the buildings, procedures, communications, and response systems around them are truly prepared?

Why must grieving parents become advocates for change after losing the most precious people in their lives?

And why do families have to keep asking the same questions after every new tragedy?

Under CM Yogi Adityanath, Uttar Pradesh has transformed from a state of neglected sports infrastructure and limited support into a true powerhouse for athletes.

Before 2017, during the SP Sarkar years, UP’s sporting ecosystem was in poor shape. Stadiums like Green Park, Babu Stadium, and others suffered from neglect, outdated facilities, slow renovations, and a lack of modern infrastructure. There was no robust policy for rewards, jobs, or grassroots talent, and the state struggled to host major events or retain talent effectively. Sports remained secondary, with athletes often facing limited opportunities and recognition.

The  decisive shift that began in 2017 under Yogi Ji’s leadership: 

from vision to action. 
Today, UP offers among the highest incentives in the country—₹6 crore for an individual Olympic gold, ₹4 crore for silver, ₹2 crore for bronze (with strong team rewards too), plus ₹10 lakh for Olympic participants and ₹5 lakh for Asian Games/Commonwealth Games participants. Medal winners receive gazetted government jobs (over 500 athletes already placed, with more underway), monthly support for coaches, kits for young athletes, and structured recognition under schemes like “Padak Lao, Pad Pao.”

Infrastructure has expanded systematically: village-level grounds, block mini-stadiums, district facilities, upgraded sports colleges, Major Dhyan Chand Sports University in Meerut, and hosting of national and international events. Grassroots talent is nurtured, coaches supported, and champions celebrated—from welcoming Asian Games gold winners like Arjun Deshwal to empowering women athletes such as Prachi Chaudhary, Parul Chaudhary, and others who bring medals for India.

This is not just policy on paper; 
it is delivering results—more medals, better training ecosystems, secure futures for athletes, and a sporting culture that prioritizes merit over recommendations. 

Where SP Sarkar left gaps in infrastructure and support, 
Yogi Sarkar has built a complete pipeline from village playgrounds to global podiums.

UP’s sporting future is brighter, stronger, and more inclusive because of this focused leadership. 

The transformation is real and visible.

#YogiAdityanath #TransformingUP #SportsSeGrowth #UttarPradeshElection2027   #UPWithYogiSarkar

--Life After Death: The Necessity of Spiritual Preparation--
People often wonder: How can one part from loved ones after death when one’s entire life revolved around them? How can the mind relinquish those very relationships that once formed the foundation of its existence?
The answer lies in understanding Maya, attachment, and the necessity of spiritual preparation.
Consider a man who meets with an accidental death. His life was deeply intertwined with his family, responsibilities, and unfulfilled desires. Having never prepared himself for this eventuality, he remains entangled in the very attachments that defined his worldly existence. After death, the Jeeva enters a state of complete Jadata, deprived of the faculties through which it once exercised its Purushartha. Its attachments persist, but the means to fulfil them are no longer available. What was once a source of happiness becomes a source of torment, for the Jeeva can neither relinquish its desires at will nor act upon them as it once could.
The tragedy lies not merely in the cessation of physical life, but in the failure to prepare for its culmination. Without the guidance of a Guru, the grace of one's Ishta, and the spiritual discipline necessary to transcend worldly attachments, the Jeeva remains bound by the very desires it never learned to overcome.
Now consider natural death. Observe an elderly person who, in his youth, was courageous, witty, assertive, and deeply involved in worldly affairs. With advancing age, his physical strength diminishes, his mental faculties weaken, and his emotional engagement with the world gradually changes. He may withdraw from family affairs, becoming seemingly aloof from the very people who once constituted the centre of his existence.
This transformation offers a glimpse into the profound transition that awaits the Jeeva in the Sukshma Jagat. The relinquishment of worldly identity, attachments, and desires is not something to be initiated at the moment of death; it is a process that must be consciously undertaken during one's lifetime. The Jeeva must prepare for this transformation while it still possesses the capacity for Purushartha.
The principle is unequivocal: the transformation must begin here, in this very life.
Do not wait for death to teach you detachment or for separation to teach you surrender. Practise Sharanagati while you still possess the ability to act, understand, and seek guidance. Surrender your ego, attachments, and sense of ownership at Maa's feet while you are alive.
This does not mean abandoning your family or evading worldly responsibilities. It means fulfilling them without becoming enslaved by possessiveness, loving without the illusion of permanence, and living in the world without allowing it to become the sole foundation of your identity.
The ultimate aspiration is to attain a peaceful place in Maa's Mandala, free from the compulsions of unfulfilled desires and established in a state of complete bliss. Such a state cannot be approached merely through a last-minute invocation; it demands a transformation of consciousness cultivated through lifelong surrender.
Do not postpone spiritual preparation until the final hour. Death does not grant you the opportunity to undo a lifetime of attachments at will. Prepare now, surrender now, and begin dissolving the illusion of individual identity at the divine feet of Maa while you are still alive.
