DON’T TOUCH MY SANCTUARY ! (Guess what happens when the one miraculous lifeline that saved a church after its biggest failure nearly two centuries ago and became its most distinctive doctrine… now threatens to become its most biblically undefendable millstone ?)  

There is a sanctuary in heaven, the true tabernacle that the Lord set up and not humans. In it Christ ministers on our behalf… In 1844, at the end of the prophetic period of 2300 days, He entered the second and last phase of His atoning ministry… It is a work of investigative judgment which is part of the ultimate disposition of all sin, typified by the cleansing of the ancient Hebrew sanctuary on the Day of Atonement.  

Adventist fundamental beliefs (1980)  

Seventh-day Adventists accept the Bible as their only creed and hold certain fundamental beliefs to be the teaching of the Holy Scriptures. These beliefs, as set forth here, constitute the church’s understanding and expression of the teaching of Scripture. Revision of these statements may be expected at a General Conference Session when the church is led by the Holy Spirit to a fuller understanding of Bible truth or finds better language in which to express the teachings of God’s Holy Word.  

Adventist fundamental beliefs (2015)  

As Adventists, many of our "unique" doctrines are not, really, unique. After all, other Christians (not many, admittedly) into greater focus. keep the seventh-day Sabbath, as well. Though a majority of the Christian world believes in the immortality of the soul, other Christians understand that the dead sleep in the grave until the resurrection, either the first or second. Various "Adventist" teachings, i.e., eternal destruction (as opposed to eternal torment) or the nature of the millennium, can be found elsewhere too. In fact, almost all our doctrines are scattered throughout Christendom.  Except one: the 1844 pre-Advent judgment. For some, this fact is worrisome; Why don't more Christians see it, as well? For others, the uniqueness of the doctrine points even more powerfully to the special calling of the Seventh-day Adventist Church. It's precisely because no one else teaches this judgment that we have been raised to do so. From this doctrine, perhaps more than any other, our distinct identity as Seventh-day Adventists arises.  

Sabbath School quarterly (2006)  

The [sanctuary] doctrine is, to me, the most colossal, psychological, face-saving phenomenon in religious history. … We personally do not believe that there is even a suspicion of a verse in Scripture to sustain such a peculiar position, and we further believe that any effort to establish it is stale, flat, and unprofitable.  

Donald Grey Barnhouse (Are Seventh-day Adventists Christians? A New Look at Seventh-Day Adventism, Eternity magazine, 1956)  

With the traditional Adventist interpretation of Daniel 8:14 as thesis, the historic-linguistic-contextual method of exegesis, which stands in opposition to it at practically every point, is its antithesis. (…) Our interpretational thesis and methodological antithesis are as impossible and mutually exclusive as matter and anti-matter and have the potential of mutually destroying each other, and the church as well. While Adventist Bible scholars have adopted the historical method, the church, as a whole, still basically practices the proof text method. Unresolved this dichotomy could have unfortunate consequences. The only way to resolve a problem such as this, is to find synthesis on a higher level of understanding.  

Raymond F. Cottrell (A Hermeneutic for Daniel 8:14, 1980)    

Time and again competent non-Adventist Bible scholars have acknowledged that there is a biblical basis for cardinal points of Adventist faith such as the Sabbath, the second Advent and the nature of man. But without exception… they denounce our interpretation of Daniel 8:14 as eisegesis of the worst sort… Seventh-day Adventists identify the sanctuary mentioned in Daniel 8:14 as the sanctuary in heaven… and they understand its cleansing as the blotting out of the confessed sins of God’s repentant people during the course of an investigative judgment, on an antitypical day of atonement that began in 1844. … Adventist teachings that cluster around Daniel 8:14 have proved to be an impassible barrier to the thoughtful consideration of the Advent message… The date 1844… is pivotal of SDA faith. Destroy these and certain conclusions are self-evident. There would be no adequate basis for the existence of SDA. … The invariable rule appears to be that the more a non-Adventist knows about the Bible, the less disposed he is to look with favor on the Adventist interpretation of Daniel 8:14… The first major incentive to devote serious attention to the problem in Daniel 8:14 arose during the course of editing the Seventh-day Adventist Bible Commentary… Within a few months after the publication of Volume 4… came the series of protracted doctrinal discussions with Walter R. Martin and Donald Grey Barnhouse. … Finally, in 1958… I wrote to 27 leading Adventist Bible scholars… All 27 responded… A careful analysis… made evident that we had no satisfactory answer to the criticisms… Not one of the 27 believed that there was a linguistic or contextual basis for applying Daniel 8:14 to the heavenly sanctuary, an antitypical day of atonement, or 1844. As a result… a select “Committee on Problems in the Book of Daniel” [was appointed]… The majority and the minority both reached the same conclusions, but by different routes. … As a result of this impasse, the committee finally agreed to issue no formal report… My study… concluded that… the sanctuary of Daniel 8:14 is the same sanctuary referred to in verses 11-13, that is, the ancient temple in Jerusalem; that the “cleansing” or “restoration”… constituted its purification and rededication after desecration by the little horn… I believe that the hermeneutical principles outlined above provided an adequate inspired basis for applying the 2,300 evenings-mornings to 2,300 literal years terminating in 1844… Let it be clearly understood that the hermeneutic here proposed in no way alters the teachings we have traditionally based on Daniel 8:14. It does not affect the content of these teachings, but the method by which they are established as truth… In arriving at these conclusions, William Miller and other early Adventists basically followed the proof text method… The proof text method is basically what Bible scholars call eisegesis… During the 1930s Adventist college Bible teachers began to make consistent use of the historical-linguistic-contextual method… By the mid-1930s we were far up a theological cul de sac… For 25 years or more, the Bible scholars of the church have been well aware of the exegetical problems our conventional interpretation of Daniel 8:14… encounters… Non-Adventist critics… object that it cannot be derived from the words of Scripture but is superimposed upon them. … The problem is clear, especially if one remembers the unanimous acknowledgment of leading Adventist biblical scholars, clearly expressed in the 1958 poll, that there is no linguistic or contextual basis for our traditional interpretation of this passage. … A conclusive case for the heavenly sanctuary and a pre-Advent judgment can be made directly from Scripture, wholly apart from Daniel 8:14 and Hebrews 9… Can we not be willing to rely on these other passages…?"  

Raymond F. Cottrell ("Sanctuary Debate: A Question of Method", 1980)  

Raymond has suggested to us a "way out" from the "dilemma" our denomination is now supposed to be caught in.  That is an escape mechanism based on a theory of the most "miraculous" our Church has ever been placed in front of.” (…) “By way of introduction, Elder Cottrell tries to convince us of the unqualified benefits our denomination has enjoyed as a direct result of one great historical event:  A new generation of Seventh-day Adventist scholars were finally blessed with the golden opportunity of education, which had been denied to our Bible students in former days.  According to Cottrell, we observed a marked improvement in the accuracy of conclusions arrived at in Adventist Bible research precisely at the time when those new scholars, with their more sophisticated knowledge, started making their impact in our offices and class rooms. Of course he does not, in this order of ideas, put any personal blame on the older researchers.  They just had the misfortune of not being properly educated.  So they were bound to come out as self-educated men, that is, men of mediocre scholarliness.  The new enlightenment we are now enjoying, as a denomination, is alleged as the positive reason for a new hope for the future.  Infallible evidence of this is a new awareness of problems our previous men of Biblical research were never confronted with.  Cottrell is referring to the increasing impossibility of harmonizing the actual contents of some contents of some Biblical texts with what our pioneers and the Spirit of Prophecy writings were once induced to put down, firmly and securely, as landmarks of our official creed. Brother Cottrell never tires of repeating that the large majority of these modern SDA Bible scholars agree wholeheartedly with him regarding the problem aspect of fundamental statements made by Ellen White in, for instance, absolutely decisive chapters of the Great Controversy.  Here Cottrell is not one bit less emphatic than Brinsmead and Ford, that objective scholarliness opens a gulf of disparity between The Bible and Ellen White. But it is in the suggested "remedy" to this situation Cottrell manifests the uniqueness of his spirit.  It is his "solution" that is without a rival in the history of Seventh-day Adventism. By and large, Protestants have never acquired any fame comparable to that of Catholics for what theology and philosophy have called "reconciliatio oppositorum" or "complexio oppositorum".  In fact it is rather secular philosophy -- and not at all traditional religion -- that has developed the habit of astonishing the world of thinking men by having the boldness to blow up the virtual problem of mutually exclusive stand-points into thin air. (…) But what is his "solution" really like then, in this concrete instance?  How does Cottrell manage to still defend the doctrine of inerrancy regarding the teachings coming to us through Ellen G. White's ministry?  Nobody, you see, is more emphatic in extolling Ellen White as the great prophetess par excellence of the people of God in the endtime.  Therefore, he says, we must accept what her message has handed down to us in terms of basic landmarks for our faith as the very truth, the full truth and nothing but the truth. But then how come that Ellen White apparently can permit herself to go so boldly against certain things the Bible says about Christ's ministry in the sanctuary?  For here, as we recall, Cottrell is more emphatic maybe than anybody else, pointing out the great superiority of, according to Cottrell, the modern research method.  The modern researchers' accurate knowledge was, according to Cottrell, arrived at for the simple reason that they applied the historicolinguistic method of exegesis.  This has led them to conclusions quite opposite to those expressed solemnly and categorically by Ellen White in the Great Controversy.  But how then can the Prophetess, with "her" now classical doctrines about 1844 and the Investigative Judgement dare to go contrary to the "evident" testimony of the Scriptures?Cottrell's explanation is scaringly simple and straightforward:  Ellen White, in her capacity as the great Prophetess of the endtime has a right to do all this.  She is divinely entitled to reinterpret prophecies of the Bible in accordance with God's special intentions in the endtime.  "Parallel instances" of this kind are referred to, for instance Paul's "innovating interpretations" of statements in the Old Testament.  To the first century Christians such OT prophecies constituted the treasury from which they had to draw.

Carsten Johnsen (1982)

The traditional interpretation of Daniel 8:14 with its sanctuary and investigative judgment, which gave birth to Seventh-day Adventism and accounts for its existence as a distinct entity within Christendom, has been the object of more criticism and debate, by both Adventists and non-Adventists, than all other facets of its belief system combined. (...) There can be no question as to the sincerity, diligence, and integrity of those who formulated the traditional Adventist interpretation of Daniel 8:14. It is equally obvious that they were following the flawed principles of the prooftext method: (1) In four major instances they adopted translation errors where the KJV misrepresents the Hebrew text. (2) They completely ignored the literary context in which Daniel 8:14 occurs. (3) They likewise ignored the historical context specified by the first six chapters and chapter 9:1-19 of the book. (...) In the years immediately following October 22, 1844 the traditional sanctuary doctrine was an important asset for stabilizing the faith of disappointed Adventists. Today it is an equally significant liability and deterrent to the faith, confidence, and salvation of biblically literate Adventists and non-Adventists alike. It was present truth following the great disappointment on October 22, 1844. It is not present truth in the year of our Lord 2002. Quod erat demonstrandum!    

Raymond F. Cottrell (The Sanctuary Doctrine – Asset or Liability?,  2002)  

Then I heard one saint speaking, and another saint said unto that certain saint which spake, How long shall be the vision concerning the daily sacrifice, and the transgression of desolation, to give both the sanctuary and the host to be trodden under foot? And he said unto me, unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed.  

Daniel 8: 13-14 (KJV)

Then I heard one angel ask another, “How long will these things that were seen in the vision continue? How long will an awful sin replace the daily sacrifices? How long will the army of heaven and the Temple be trampled on?” I heard the other angel answer, “It will continue for 2,300 evenings and mornings, during which sacrifices will not be offered. Then the Temple will be restored.  

Daniel 8: 13-14 (Good News)   

And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.   

Genesis 1:5  

And he shall make an atonement for the holy place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and because of their transgressions in all their sins.   

Leviticus 16:16   

Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary. (...) But into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood, which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people. (...) But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands… Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.  

Hebrews 9: 1-12  

But the court which is without the temple leave out, and measure it not; for it is given unto the Gentiles: and the holy city shall they tread under foot forty and two months. And I will give power unto my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy a thousand two hundred and threescore days, clothed in sackcloth. (...) And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days. And to the woman were given two wings of a great eagle, that she might fly into the wilderness, into her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, from the face of the serpent.  (...) And there was given unto him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies; and power was given unto him to continue forty and two months.  

Revelation 1: 2-13:5  

But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only.  

Jesus (Matthew 24:36)   

But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father.  Jesus (Mark 13:32)  It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.  

Acts 1: 7  

The king had sent letters by messengers unto Jerusalem and the cities of Juda that they should follow the strange laws of the land, And forbid burnt offerings, and sacrifice, and drink offerings, in the temple; and that they should profane the sabbaths and festival days (…) Now the 15th day of the month Casleu, in the 145th year, they set up the abomination of desolation upon the altar, and builded idol altars throughout the cities of Juda on every side; And burnt incense at the doors of their houses, and in the streets. And when they had rent in pieces the books of the law which they found, they burnt them with fire. And whosoever was found with any the book of the testament, or if any committed to the law, the king's commandment was, that they should put him to death. (…) Now the 25th day of the month they did sacrifice upon the idol altar, which was upon the altar of God.  

1 Maccabees 1:44–59  

Now on the 25th day of the 9th month, which is called the month Casleu, in the 148th year, they rose up betimes in the morning, And offered sacrifice according to the law upon the new altar of burnt offerings, which they had made. Look, at what time and what day the heathen had profaned it, even in that was it dedicated with songs, and citherns, and harps, and cymbals.  

1 Maccabees 4:52–54  

These things were done on the very same day on which their Divine worship had fallen off, and was reduced to a profane and common use, after three years’ time; for so it was, that the temple was made desolate by Antiochus, and so continued for three years. This desolation happened to the temple in the 145th year, on the 25th day of the month Apeliens… but it was dedicated anew, on the same day, the 25th of the month Apeliens, on the 148th year.  

Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 12.316–320)  

Antiochus, called Epiphanes, on defeating the Jews had entered the innermost sanctuary of the god’s temple… he sacrificed before the image of the founder and the open-air altar of the god a great sow, and poured its blood over them. Then… he ordered that their holy books… should be sprinkled with the broth of the meat; that the lamp… which burns continually in the temple should be extinguished; and that the high priest and the rest of the Jews should be compelled to partake of the meat.  

Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 34/35.1.3–5)  

Unto two thousand and three hundred evenings, mornings] i.e. successive evenings and mornings: cf. Daniel 8:26 -the vision of the evenings and the mornings." The expression is peculiar; but it seems to have been suggested by the fact that the burnt-offering (Daniel 8:11; Daniel 8:13) was offered morning and evening daily (Exodus 29:38-42); the meaning consequently is that this offering would cease for 2300 times, i.e. during 1150 days (...). In Daniel 7:25 (...), Daniel 12:7, the period of persecution is to last 31/2 years, i.e. (if the year be reckoned at 360 days) 1260 days, or, if account be taken of the varying possibilities of the Calendar in use in the 2nd century b.c., 1274 or 1309 days; and, according to 1Ma 1:54; 1Ma 4:52-53, the interval which actually elapsed between the erection of the heathen altar upon the altar of burnt-offering, on the 15th of Chisleu, b.c. 168, and the dedication of the new altar on the 25th of Chisleu, b.c. 165, was 3 years and 10 days (i.e. 1090, 1102 3, or 1132 3 days). The period assigned here is some months less than 31/2 years; it is not however identified with the entire period of the persecution, but only with that part of it during which the daily sacrifice was interrupted and the Temple desecrated. It seems therefore (cf. Daniel 12:11) that 15 Chisleu b.c. 168 must be the terminus a quo, the end of the period assigned not agreeing precisely with the event.  By some commentators the expression -evening, morning" has been understood as equivalent to day (cf. Genesis 1:5, Genesis 1:8)  

Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges  

Dear Mr. Lynch, you have been misinformed “that the only correct translation of Dan 8:14 is ‘until 2,300 days.’” The Hebrew phrase can only mean ‘For 2,300 evenings and mornings,’ which equals 1,150 days. I know of no one who translates the phrase 2,300 days. Genesis 1 is not relevant to this phrase…. the reference is to the 1,150 evening and 1,150 morning sacrifices.  

Alexander A. Di Lella (1958)  

Twenty-seven of our top men in language and exegesis. All twenty-seven replied that it was impossible to make a linguistic connection between Dan. 8:14 and Lev. 16. There is no Biblical basis for assuming that the year-day be applied to Dan. 8 and 9.   

Desmond Ford (1980)  

The phrase ʿereb bōqer (“evening morning”) in Daniel 8:14 is widely understood by critical commentators as referring to the interruption of the daily morning and evening sacrifices. 2,300 such offerings equal 1,150 days (roughly three years), matching the historical desecration of the temple under Antiochus IV Epiphanes (c. 167–164 BCE). (...) The Greek and Latin versions mistakenly read twenty-three hundred days.  John J. Collins (Hermeneia, 1993)  Thus Dan 8:14 has nothing to do with the high priestly ministry of Christ or an extended chronology ending in 1844. In the context of Daniel, it is a forecast of how long the Jerusalem Temple would linger in a desecrated state… during the reign of Antiochus IV.   

Jerry Gladson (2017)  

When Antiochus IV and the Greeks arrive, and they conquer Jerusalem, they defile the temple, as we know from the proper story of Hanukkah. They bring the knowledge with them. Why do they have the knowledge? Because these roof tiles, or at least modern roof tiles, were invented in the seventh century B.C., in the middle of Greece itself, and then spread around the world, but never to the Middle East." (…) We can date each strata about the contents of that strata. And, for the most part, it depends on the pottery itself. We know that during certain periods, certain types of pottery, meaning vessels, pottery vessels were used. In this case, it was really both the coins and the pottery itself that showed us that the strata or the layer where these roof tiles were found was sealed in the second century B.C.E., so we know that couldn't have been later. (…) Weinberger proved that the material is local, the clay is local, from an area west of Jerusalem called the Motza … with the addition of sand and straw, which are also local. (…) Other than the Acra, this fortress, these roof tiles are also very clear proof for the presence of the Greeks during the same time period. The first book of Maccabees describes the arrival of the Greeks, Antiochus IV and the struggle. And then much later tradition talks about the defilement of the temple and the miracle of the oil and eight days. That's why today all the Jews celebrate Hanukkah, but we have never really had real material proof for the presence of the Greeks themselves.  

Dr. Filip Vukosavović (2023)  

During archaeological excavations operated by the Israel Antiquities Authority and Tel-Aviv University, 16 pieces of ceramic roof tiles were discovered. (…) The tiles discovered (...) in City of David National Park date back to the time period of Greek Seleucid King Antiochus IV Epiphanes. MAJOR GENERAL CHRIS OLUKOLADE (RTD), FNIPR, mni

Some military officers become known for their battlefield commands. Others leave their mark through the responsibility of communicating the Armed Forces' activities to the nation.

Major General Chris Olukolade is a familiar name in Nigeria's military public relations history.

Olukolade served in the Nigerian Army and rose to the rank of Major General. His career included important responsibilities in military communication, public information and institutional representation.

He became Director of Defence Information in March 2013, placing him at the forefront of communication between the Nigerian Armed Forces, the media and the public during a challenging period in the nation's security history.

Before his retirement, he also served as chairman of the Forum of Spokespersons on Security and Response Agencies, promoting cooperation among the communication representatives of Nigeria's security and emergency institutions.

In July 2015, Olukolade announced his retirement from the military. He was succeeded as Director of Defence Information by Colonel Rabe Abubakar, who assumed the position in August 2015.

His departure marked the end of a prominent chapter in Nigeria's military communications landscape.

Military service extends beyond operational deployments. Communicating official information, addressing public concerns and maintaining effective media relations are also important responsibilities.

Major General Chris Olukolade's career offers an opportunity to recognise the officers who served in this demanding space, where accuracy, institutional responsibility and public understanding matter.

text:
15-10-2026 Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models : https://t.co/uD7GWrha4w

"Weijian LuoEqual contribution.Project leader: pkulwj1994@icloud.comDots Studio, XiaohongshuYujian Chen1Polyadic Research GroupPeking UniversityHao JiangPolyadic Research GroupSAGA Lab, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, ShenzhenGuang ChengThe University of California, Los AngelesTianyang HuCorresponding author: hutianyang@cuhk.edu.cnPolyadic Research GroupSAGA Lab, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
Abstract
Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT ), combining feature and query–key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model’s underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.
Figure 1:Architectural ablations during training on OWT-1024. GenPPL (left) and mean per-sample unigram entropy (right) at 128 NFEs, using 1,024 samples and EMA weights. R1 (baseline) and R7 (full model) are shown through 180k updates. For clarity, trajectories for R2–R6 are shown only through 50k updates. Points are unsmoothed logged measurements; endpoints are labeled at 180k. Legend additions are cumulative, with wider conditioning preceding shortcut detachment (Table 4). Lower GenPPL is accompanied by lower unigram entropy; checkpoint steps and sample counts are stated separately for each comparison.
1Introduction
Autoregressive language models generate text by predicting tokens sequentially. Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative: they jointly refine continuous representations of a token sequence through iterative denoising or flow dynamics, allowing multiple token positions to be updated in parallel. Recent studies have explored a range of representations, training objectives, and generative dynamics, including one-hot flows, learned token embeddings, and latent-space models (Lee et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Meshchaninov et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026). Despite their different formulations, these models share a central computational component: a neural backbone that maps noisy continuous states to predictions for language generation.Figure 2:Generation results on OWT (L=1024). (a) Baseline and LangDiT at 128/1,024 denoising steps using checkpoints within 250k updates. The LangFlow comparisons use 250k checkpoints at 128 NFE and 180k checkpoints at 1,024 NFE. RePlaID compares 40k versus 150k at 128 steps and 220k versus 250k at 1,024 steps, so these pairs do not match training progress; the latter also differs in planned budget. (b) Extended-training checkpoints: LangFlow 660k and RePlaID 520k from 1M-update plans. RePlaID requires one final denoiser call beyond the displayed step count. Bars show GenPPL; bracketed values show mean per-sample unigram entropy. All results use 1,024 samples and EMA weights; † denotes our implementation (Table 3).
Much of the progress in CDLMs has focused on the formulation and learning of continuous generative processes, while the Transformer architectures that implement them have received comparatively less systematic attention. Existing models commonly inherit architectural choices from causal large language models (LLMs) or from Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) developed for image generation. These architectures provide useful starting points for methodological research, but their suitability for continuous language generation warrants closer examination. Causal LLMs are designed for next-token prediction, whereas image DiTs operate on continuous visual representations. CDLMs must recover discrete language tokens from noisy continuous states while coordinating noise-dependent computation, vocabulary prediction, and, when used, self-conditioning. These requirements motivate a central question:
•What Transformer architecture is best suited to continuous diffusion language models?In this paper, we systematically study Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce LangDiT , a backbone designed for continuous language generation. Our central finding is that architectural choices effective in causal LLMs or image diffusion models do not necessarily yield the best performance in CDLMs. By varying the architecture within fixed model formulations, we show that architectural design can substantially improve generation performance. We first develop and evaluate LangDiT within LangFlow (Chen et al., 2026), then transfer it to Plaid-style CDLMs (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Yang et al., 2026). In each setting, we retain the underlying representation, objective formulation, and inference sampler to study architectural changes within each formulation. The Plaid adaptation reuses a subset of the design while retaining its native prediction interface.We investigate three aspects of CDLM architecture. Within the backbone, we study how feature normalization and noise conditioning affect denoising. At the vocabulary interface, we examine how gradients through the likelihood shortcut affect the learning of token embeddings. For self-conditioning, we investigate how strongly previous predictions should guide subsequent denoising. A cumulative ablation study under shared training and evaluation settings measures the incremental effects of these components, leading to a reusable architecture that improves generation while preserving the underlying model formulation.We evaluate LangDiT on OpenWebText unconditional generation at a sequence length of 1,024. A seven-stage LangFlow ladder tracks successive architectural changes (Figure 1). At 250k updates and 128 NFE under the same schedule, GenPPL decreases from 64.26 to 53.66, while mean per-sample unigram entropy changes from 5.416 to 5.391. Separately, a 660k LangFlow checkpoint and a 520k Plaid checkpoint from 1M-update plans reach GenPPL 21.72 and 11.33 at the larger sampling budget (Table 3). These extended-training scores accompany larger changes in entropy and do not isolate the effect of architecture from training budget. We distinguish these settings throughout the paper (Figure 2).Our contributions are threefold:
•We conduct a systematic empirical study of six denoiser-design interventions in CDLMs, using a cumulative LangFlow ablation under shared training and evaluation settings.
•We introduce LangDiT , which combines backbone normalization and noise conditioning with likelihood-shortcut gradient routing, calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning.
•We demonstrate lower GenPPL in matched LangFlow comparisons and examine the reuse of compatible components in a Plaid-style formulation, reporting sampling cost and unigram entropy alongside generation perplexity.Together, these findings establish architectural design as an important source of progress in CDLMs and provide a reusable foundation for further research on parallel language generation.
2Related Work

Continuous language diffusion and flow.
Diffusion-LM and self-conditioned embedding diffusion established continuous denoising approaches to language generation (Li et al., 2022; Strudel et al., 2022), while CDCD and Plaid developed categorical diffusion and likelihood-based training (Dieleman et al., 2022; Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023). Recent work explores flow maps (Lee et al., 2026), learned embeddings with information-based noise scheduling (Chen et al., 2026), architectural refinements (Yang et al., 2026), hyperspherical dynamics (Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026), and embedding-space flow matching (Hu et al., 2026). We study architectural design within fixed LangFlow and Plaid-style formulations.
Latent representations and decoding.
CoDAR uses contextual autoregressive decoding (Shen et al., 2026), while LDLM jointly learns an encoder, denoiser, and decoder with controlled gradient interactions (Meshchaninov et al., 2026). Cola-DLM introduces a text VAE and latent prior (Guo et al., 2026), and AURORA-LM restricts the noisy-input pathway while preserving high-capacity latents (Liang et al., 2026). Analysis of ELF links token recovery to decoder margins and denoising trajectories (Du and Ma, 2026). Our changes operate within the existing codebook-based prediction interface.
Normalization and conditioning.
DiT and EDM2 emphasize adaptive conditioning and magnitude control in diffusion networks (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Karras et al., 2024). RMSNorm, nGPT, and query–key normalization provide complementary approaches to controlling representation and attention scales (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019; Loshchilov et al., 2025; Henry et al., 2020). Related work examines attention-entropy collapse (Zhai et al., 2023) and uses query–key RMSNorm in rectified-flow Transformers (Esser et al., 2024). We examine these normalization choices alongside noise-conditioning capacity in continuous language denoising.
Self-conditioning.
Analog Bits, self-conditioned embedding diffusion, and LangFlow use previous predictions to guide denoising (Chen et al., 2022; Strudel et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2026). AURORA-LM addresses training–inference mismatch through trajectory consistency (Liang et al., 2026). Our entropy-based gate regulates bootstrap inputs during training while retaining the baseline loss formulation and inference sampler.
Discrete diffusion and evaluation.
MDLM, LLaDA, and iLLaDA advance masked diffusion language modeling (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2026), while Duo connects uniform-state discrete diffusion to an underlying Gaussian process (Sahoo et al., 2025). Across diffusion families, likelihood rankings can differ from those based on generation quality and sampling cost (Sahoo et al., 2026); lower GenPPL can also accompany reduced distributional coverage (Franca and Tong, 2026). We therefore report GenPPL alongside mean per-sample unigram entropy, with explicit sampling budgets.
3The Language Diffusion Transformer
LangDiT is a Transformer denoiser for continuous language generation. Its design addresses three components of denoising: processing noisy embeddings, predicting discrete tokens, and incorporating previous predictions through self-conditioning. We develop the architecture within a LangFlow-style baseline (Chen et al., 2026), retaining its continuous representation, training and noise-schedule objective formulations, and inference sampler across architectural variants. Table 1 summarizes the design choices.Table 1:Architectural design principles and their implementation in LangDiT .ComponentDesign principleImplementationBackboneSeparate feature-scale control from noise-dependent modulation.Backbone and Q/K RMSNorm; wider noise conditioning.Vocabulary headControl the shortcut’s forward contribution and direct codebook gradients separately.Shortcut detachment; bounded learned calibration.Self-conditioningDistinguish clean-state estimation from auxiliary feedback during training.Confidence-gated bootstrap inputs; unweighted posterior-mean estimates at inference.

3.1Overall Denoising Pipeline
At each denoising step, an input projection combines noisy token embeddings zγ with an optional self-conditioning estimate xSC. A bidirectional Transformer processes the sequence through attention and feed-forward sublayers modulated by the noise level γ. An untied vocabulary head produces contextual logits, augmented by a gated likelihood shortcut that measures compatibility between the noisy state and the codebook. Softmax yields token probabilities, whose weighted embedding mean provides the clean-state estimate used for both sampler updates and subsequent self-conditioning. Figure 3(a) illustrates this pipeline with one Transformer block expanded.Relative to the baseline, LangDiT introduces backbone RMSNorm for feature-scale control, query–key RMSNorm for attention-logit scale control, and wider noise conditioning for greater modulation capacity. The likelihood shortcut follows a Gaussian noise model (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). We detach its embedding matrix to block the direct codebook-gradient path, while a bounded gate controls its forward contribution. An entropy-based gate further regulates bootstrap self-conditioning during training (Figure 3(b)); inference retains the un-gated posterior-mean estimator for both self-conditioning and sampler updates.Figure 3:Transformer architecture and self-conditioning in LangDiT . (a) The denoiser is read from bottom to top, with one of 12 blocks expanded. RMSNorm precedes each modulated sublayer; headwise query–key RMSNorm precedes RoPE, while values undergo neither operation. The 256-dimensional noise embedding supplies modulation parameters and residual gates (dashed arrows). A gated likelihood shortcut bypasses the Transformer and its untied vocabulary head. Only the shortcut’s explicit codebook factor is detached; C=s​E~ remains trainable through noisy-state construction. (b) A bootstrap call to the same denoiser produces token probabilities without gradient tracking. These probabilities determine a clean-state estimate and an entropy-based weight for training self-conditioning (Equation (13)). Inference passes the unweighted estimate to the next step. Shortcut warmup is omitted for clarity.

The Green Ribbon

Part 1 : The Years That Belonged to Them

He remembered the classroom window...

During the monsoon, its wooden frame swelled, and they could close it only by pushing together. She counted to three. He always pushed at two, just to see her turn with that little frown she could never keep.

He remembered the extra dosa she brought because Ammamma packed fruit for him and he often forgot to eat. She placed the larger half on his side of the tiffin lid. When she forgot, he looked so miserable that she called him a greedy buffalo and shared hers.

On the school bus, she taught him fractions while he watched raindrops racing down the glass.

“You aren't listening.”
“I am.”
“Three-fourths of twelve?”
“Nine.”
“Occasionally, you know things.”

Their notebooks held secrets no one else understood. She corrected his spelling and drew tiny mangoes beside his sums. He drew the hills beyond their village and once, a house with two figures outside.

“Why am I so short?”
“Because you are.”

She took his pencil and made herself taller. He never changed it back.

He remembered Pari, her golden retriever puppy, waiting at the bend with muddy paws and a wildly wagging tail. She greeted the girl first, then buried her nose in his palm.

“She loves me more,” the girl insisted.
“She came to me twice.”
“Because you smell of my dosa.”

Pari followed them everywhere, squeezing between their legs and stealing their slippers. Sometimes the girl scolded her, and he secretly slipped the puppy another piece of food.

On Sundays, they collected fallen mangoes from Ammamma's garden. She always chose the ripest ones for him, pretending she preferred the sour ones herself. Once he caught her making a face after biting into one.

“You don't like sour mangoes.”
“I do.”
“Then why are you crying?”
“Because you're irritating.”

He laughed so hard that she threw a mango leaf at him.

He remembered those afternoons more clearly than many things that came afterwards. Her bare feet on the wet veranda, the smell of coconut oil in her hair, Pari asleep with her head resting on his schoolbag. Sometimes they sat without speaking, watching the rain fill the little channels along the courtyard.

He had never wondered why silence felt so comfortable beside her.

It simply did.

During heavy rain, they did homework on Ammamma's veranda. Once thunder sent Pari trembling beneath the bench. The girl gathered her into her arms, but when lightning flashed, her own fingers shook.

“Are you frightened too?” “No.”

He sat beside her and offered his hand.
“You can hold mine until Pari feels better.”

She took it.

“Pari is very frightened,” she whispered. “I know.”

He remembered how long she held on.

He remembered the afternoon she fell while running after Pari. Her knee was bleeding, and she was furious with herself for crying. He fetched water, washed away the dirt, and tore a clean strip from his handkerchief to cover the scrape.

“Don't tell anyone I cried.” “I didn't see you cry.” “You're looking at me.” “I'm looking at your knee.”

She laughed through her tears. Later, when his own hand was scratched climbing a mango tree, she insisted on tying the remaining piece of his handkerchief around it.

And he remembered the green ribbon.
It had come loose on the bus, and she turned her back towards him.
“Tie it.”
His first knot slipped. The second pulled her hair. When he finished, the ribbon hung crookedly against her braid.
“That's terrible.” “It won't fall.”

Her mother offered to retie it that evening. She refused. The next morning she wore the same ribbon, still crooked.
He had noticed only that it was green.

He remembered her saving him the last piece of mango, defending him when another boy called him stupid, and waiting at the bus stop even when the rain soaked her shoes.

“Pari was looking for you,” she would say. “Only Pari?” “Don't be silly.”

He always took her schoolbag, even after its broken strap had been repaired.

In 1869, Napoleon III offered a prize to anyone who could make a cheap butter substitute for his navy and for the poor.

A French chemist named Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès won it. He blended beef fat with milk and called it oleomargarine.

Later, beef fat was swapped for vegetable oils. Liquid oil doesn't spread, so factories hardened it with hydrogen gas.

That process made trans fats.

For decades, hard margarine was sold as the heart-friendly choice over butter.

In 2015, the US FDA ruled that partially hydrogenated oils were no longer "generally recognised as safe." 

In 2018, the WHO launched a plan to remove industrial trans fats from the world's food supply.

The spread was a substitute that got marketed as an upgrade.

Butter is cream. It still is.

text:
In the early hours of 16 October 1793 she wrote a last letter to her sister-in-law Madame Élisabeth (imprisoned separately). 

It expressed calm, asserted her innocence, regretted abandoning her children, offered blessings, and affirmed her Catholic faith. The letter never reached Élisabeth (who was later executed). 

Marie Antoinette was taken by cart to the Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde), her hair cut, hands bound, and guillotined at about noon. She was 37. 

Her body was initially buried in a common grave; after the Bourbon Restoration it was reinterred at the Basilica of Saint-Denis with Louis XVI. 

“Children and Aftermath”
Only one child survived to adulthood: Marie-Thérèse Charlotte, released in 1795, and later known as the Duchesse d’Angoulême. She lived in exile much of her life and died in 1851. 

Louis-Charles (recognized by royalists as Louis XVII) died in the Temple prison in 1795, age 10, of illness worsened by harsh conditions. DNA testing of a preserved heart, later confirmed his identity and death in prison. 

Louis-Joseph had already died in 1789; Sophie in 1787.
Myths and Context
The famous line “Let them eat cake” (“Qu’ils mangent de la brioche”) is not hers. 

A similar anecdote appears in Rousseau’s Confessions (written years earlier, referring to a “great princess”), and the specific attribution to Marie Antoinette arose decades after her death. 

There is no contemporary evidence she said it. Hostile propaganda, her Austrian birth, real court spending, and the political crisis of the late 1780s shaped her image far more than any single quotation. 

She was neither a pure villain of excess nor a simple martyr. 

She was a young woman placed in a political marriage, shaped by court culture, loyal to her family and husband, and ultimately destroyed by the Revolution’s radicalization and years of defamatory propaganda. Her execution on 16 October 1793 closed one chapter of the French monarchy.

text:
Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access is not an attempt to challenge Eritrea’s sovereignty or lay claim to its territory. It is a matter of Ethiopia’s legitimate national interest and strategic necessity, one that can be addressed through peaceful negotiations and mutually beneficial arrangements.
When Ethiopia reached an agreement with Somaliland to secure access to the sea, Eritrea opposed it. Its position on Red Sea affairs, including its insistence that governance of the Red Sea should be restricted to coastal states, raises a fundamental question: On what principle does Eritrea oppose Ethiopia’s legitimate aspiration to secure sea access?
If Eritrea’s position offers no viable alternative for Ethiopia and instead focuses on preventing Ethiopia from securing access to the sea through peaceful means, such a stance contradicts the principles of good neighbourliness, regional cooperation, and shared development.
Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access should not be treated as a justification for territorial conflict with Eritrea. However, just as Eritrea expects its own sovereignty to be respected, it must also refrain from policies that undermine Ethiopia’s legitimate national interests. The future stability of the region will not be secured by one country denying another its legitimate interests, but by pursuing solutions through dialogue, mutual understanding, and mutually beneficial cooperation.

text:
Pangasinense mother crafts seashell scraps into world-class home decors
By Hilda Austria
MALASIQUI, Pangasinan – A mother from the coastal Pangasinan city of Alaminos has turned discarded seashells into world-class home décor and kitchen accents, now on display at the Manila Furnishings and Apparel Manufacturers' Exchange (FAME).
Gemma Vistro of Gemma's Souvenirs began making souvenir items around in 1996 to help her husband earn income for their growing family.
"We live in Alaminos City, where the Hundred Islands National Park is, and there are a lot of tourists, and souvenir making is one of the rising livelihoods, and so I also tried to do it," she said in a phone interview Friday.
She then began selling her handmade souvenirs made from seashells, collected from the shores and some also bought from fisherfolk, going around carrying a bilao (circular basket).
"When I had enough money, I bought a bicycle with a sidecar, which helped me get around the city," she said.
Her small souvenir-making venture became a hit when a hotel offered her the chance to open a small shop.
"That's when it really took off. I also started selling souvenir T-shirts as an additional offering to tourists," she said.
Vistro said her business helped send their children to college.
Three of her four children are now graduates and working.
Two of them are respiratory therapists and one is a medical technologist, while the youngest is a fourth year civil engineering student.
Vistro still dreams of getting her souvenirs abroad.
"It is my dream to export my seashell products to other countries. The Department of Trade and Industry and Ma'am Arlyn Guico's Project Abound have helped me turn this dream into reality," she said.
She was tapped by the provincial government last year to join the Manila FAME.
"Joining Manila FAME has opened opportunities for me since through it, I was able to join Likhang Pinoy and got orders, which were brought to Japan," she said.
Her seashell plate chargers reached Japan and her fridge magnets were brought as tokens to an expo in China.
Gemma's Souvenirs added oyster-shell bag charms and keychains, as advised by mentors and designers from Project Abound, to its seashell plate chargers, lamps, jewelry holders, and other home decors.
Government support
“We support our MSMEs (micro, small and medium enterprises) and promote our Pangasinan-made products. They are on par with other export-oriented MSMEs, so we are proud," DTI Ilocos Region Assistant Director Natalia Dalaten said in an interview Thursday.
Dalaten said the DTI and provincial government, with help from Project Abound, a Pangasinan social enterprise and mentorship initiative founded by Arlyn Grace Guico, selected the Manila FAME participants.
Project Abound trains local artisans, MSMEs, and food producers to access national and international markets.
Guico said they provide guidance to MSMEs, together with the DTI, while the provincial government provides everything else they need to succeed.
She also urged the other MSMEs to persevere in their business, noting that they can only do so much, but the real work and perseverance will come from the MSMEs.
"I hope and pray you have the will and determination to improve your products. No matter how much we want to help, we can't do anything if you don't follow through or truly want us there for you," she said. (PNA)

INTERNATIONAL TRADE FAIR. Gemma Vistro (center) of Gemma's Souvenirs poses with visitors to the Manila FAME at World Trade Center in Pasay City in this undated photo. Vistro, a mother from the coastal city of Alaminos, Pangasinan, has turned discarded seashells into world-class home decorations and kitchen accents. (Photo courtesy of Pangasinan PIO)

text:
BFAR prepares Southern Leyte communities ahead of sardines fishing ban 

By Sarwell Meniano

TACLOBAN CITY – The regional office of the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) here has intensified its information campaign on the sardines fishing ban in Southern Leyte ahead of the implementation of the closed fishing season within the Fisheries Management Area (FMA) 9 beginning Dec. 1.

In a statement on Friday, BFAR emphasized the need to communicate truthful and reliable information about the three-month closed season, which will affect economic activities in fishing communities. 

The sardines closed fishing season in FMA 9, which will be observed annually from Dec. 1 to March 1 of the succeeding year, prohibits the use of specified fishing gear for catching sardines. 

From March 2 to Nov. 30, fishing activities will be subject to limited fishing days to reduce fishing pressure and support the recovery and long-term sustainability of sardine stocks.

“We have been strengthening coordination among stakeholders and improving the dissemination of accurate and timely information on fisheries conservation, government programs, and livelihood assistance for affected fishing communities,” the BFAR-Eastern Visayas said.

The measure aims to conserve sardine stocks and sustain fisheries resources in FMA 9, particularly in the 13 local government units in Southern Leyte: Maasin City, Macrohon, Malitbog, Padre Burgos, Tomas Oppus, Bontoc, Sogod, Libagon, Liloan, Pintuyan, San Francisco, San Ricardo, and Limasawa.

For three months, catching, landing, or selling sardines, including fry and juveniles, will be strictly prohibited. The measure also bans the harvest, landing, or sale of sardines measuring below 14 centimeters to allow the species to reproduce and rebuild its population.

With the closed season, BFAR offers alternative sources of income available through the Philippine Fisheries and Coastal Resiliency Project, its regular programs, other special projects, and potential livelihood assistance through convergence initiatives with partner national government agencies. 

“BFAR emphasized the importance of public awareness and compliance with fisheries regulations, as violations may result in administrative penalties, including fines and confiscation of catch and fishing gear, as well as imprisonment upon conviction, as provided by applicable laws,” the agency added.

FMA 9 spans 2.8 million hectares across 11 provinces in five regions, including parts of Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, and Caraga. (PNA)

text: JX Advanced Metals is projected to expand its semiconductor sputtering target operating profit from ¥26bn in FY2024 to ¥83bn in FY2028, lifting operating margins from 27% to 36%, according to UBS. The company holds a 60% global market share in sputtering targets used in wafer metallization. Target shipment volumes are forecast to grow 24% in 2026, 21% in 2027, and 22% in 2028, far exceeding UBS projections for 12-inch wafer volume growth of 11%, 14.5%, and 12.9%. This structural divergence is driven by advanced logic scaling, where leading-edge devices require around 20 wiring layers as industry N3 capacity reaches 293 kwpm and N2 capacity reaches 312 kwpm by end-2028. Stacking DRAM in HBM via through-silicon vias and larger interposers for redistribution layers further multiply target consumption. Profitability is set to benefit from a richer product mix and factory automation. As shrinking line widths cause conventional tantalum barrier layers to increase resistance, the industry is shifting toward manganese alloys that form thinner barriers, matching the company's high-purity target portfolio. In manufacturing, the legacy Isohara Works relies on manual cart transport, whereas the new Hitachinaka Factory starting up in 2027 introduces automated robotic lines designed to cut unit costs and export efficiency across operations. UBS models segment revenue growing from ¥94bn in FY2024 to ¥232bn in FY2028. The primary observable risk is customer qualification timing for automated lines at Hitachinaka, whereas mid-contract price revisions at annual renewals offer unmodeled upside. #Commodities #Materials Report date: 2026-10-15

We examine whether LLMs can serve as a reproducible and scalable mechanism to make comparative assessments of the quality of XAI explanations. We introduce XAI-Arena, an LLM-as-a-judge framework for scalable, reproducible, multidimensional, and stakeholder-sensitive evaluation of XAI explanation quality. XAI-Arena then allows us to compare XAI explanations along various dimensions, namely, perceived simplicity, clarity, task adequacy, trust calibration, actionability, transparency, faithfulness, and overall interpretability. We then benchmark XAI explanation methods across various datasets, machine learning models, and stakeholder personas. Human validation shows a strong positive association between LLM-generated and human ratings (Spearman’s ?? = .693, ?? < .001). Together, LLM-based evaluations can capture systematic differences in XAI explanation quality and provide a scalable and reproducible framework for comparative assessment of XAI explanations. Artificial intelligence; Machine learning; Additional Key Words and Phrases: Explainable AI, explanation quality, interpretability, user study, LLM-as-a-judge, human-centered evaluation, stakeholder perspectives, reproducibility 1 Introduction Understanding how machine learning models arrive at their predictions is essential in many practical applications. The underlying reasons may be legal, organizational, or technical, such as ensuring regulatory compliance, auditing model decisions, understanding and improving model behavior, or building trust among managers and end users. One way to achieve this is through explainable AI (XAI), which provides explanations for model predictions [1, 19, 30]. XAI helps users examine model behavior [55], identify and debug model issues [4], and communicate why a model produced a specific output [46]. However, evaluating the quality of XAI explanations remains challenging [45]. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgment, which can provide rich insights but is costly to collect and difficult to scale [9, 39, 46]. Moreover, human judgment can vary due to differences in tasks or expertise of participants [13, 33, 47]. Automated proxy metrics provide a more scalable alternative, but typically measure narrow technical properties, such as fidelity [19], stability [2], and completeness [50, 65], rather than broader dimensions of explanation quality. In particular, it is unclear whether such proxy metrics align with how stakeholders perceive or use XAI explanations [50, 65]. As a result, comparative assessments of XAI explanation quality often remain difficult to conduct in a systematic and reproducible manner. Below, we provide a short overview of existing (1) key XAI methods, (2) evaluation strategies to assess explanation quality, and (3) recent applications following the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm. 2.1 Explainable AI Methods We survey key XAI methods2 while we refer readers to [1, 30, 48] for more comprehensive overviews. Common methods in practice include: (i) SHAP [42], which uses Shapley values from cooperative game theory to attribute feature importance consistently across models; (ii) LIME [53], which fits local surrogate models around individual predictions to approximate model behavior; (iii) counterfactual explanations such as DiCE [49], which identify minimal input changes needed to alter the model’s output; and (iv) global visualization techniques such as PDP [25, 29] and permutation importance [11, 24]. PDP illustrates how model predictions change with respect to individual features, while permutation importance measures the contribution of each feature to the overall predictive accuracy [11, 32, 48, 63]. In this paper, we focus on five widely used methods (SHAP, LIME, DiCE, PDP, and permutation importance), which represent complementary explanation paradigms used in practice. One difference is that some explain individual predictions locally, while others summarize overall model behavior globally. They also vary in representation (textual, visual, or hybrid) and abstraction level, ranging from feature-level explanations to higher-level summaries of model behavior. 2.2 Evaluation of XAI Explanations Despite extensive research on XAI methods, systematic comparative evaluations of explanation quality remain limited [3, 18, 27]. Existing studies often focus on specific methods, tasks, or evaluation settings, which makes it difficult to assess how explanation quality varies across machine learning models, datasets, explanation methods, output formats, and stakeholders. For instance, an attribution method that yields clear and stable explanations for a linear model may produce noisier or less interpretable explanations in a highly nonlinear setting [60]. This motivates the development of XAI-Arena as a comparative evaluation framework in this paper. Several dimensions can be used to assess the quality of XAI explanations. Early work emphasized two main outcomes: faithfulness, which captures how accurately an explanation reflects the model’s reasoning, and interpretability, which captures how understandable it is for human users [19, 27]. Subsequent research expanded these perspectives into broader, multidimensional frameworks that combine technical and human-centered criteria, including clarity, completeness, plausibility, and usefulness [17, 31, 34, 39, 46]. Building on this line of work, we adopt eight complementary evaluation dimensions: 1 perceived simplicity, 2 clarity, 3 task adeqacy, 4 trust calibration, 5 actionability, 6 transparency, 7 faithfulness, and 8 interpretability. Note that we use perceived simplicity rather than perceived complexity so that higher ratings consistently indicate better explanation quality. Together, these dimensions should enable a comprehensive assessment of XAI explanation quality. Existing human-centered evaluations of XAI explanations vary widely in design and methodology. A common choice is to rely on user studies in which participants rate explanation quality on Likert scales, perform decision 2We use the term explanation broadly to refer to any output produced by an XAI method. Participants typically include both domain experts and non-experts, whose interpretations depend on prior technical experience and task framing [20, 39, 46]. However, broad role- or expertise-based categories may obscure differences in stakeholder knowledge and explanation needs [64]. While such studies provide fine-grained insights into how users interpret XAI explanations and calibrate trust in model predictions, they are expensive, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce at scale. Proxy metrics provide automated, quantitative measures for evaluating XAI explanations without human input [19, 50]. Fidelity-based measures assess how closely an explanation aligns with model behavior, while criteria such as completeness, stability, sensitivity, MoRF (Most Relevant First), and compactness capture different technical aspects of explanation quality [2, 50]. For example, MoRF evaluates how strongly the model output changes when the most important input features are removed [54], and stability measures how XAI explanations change under small variations in the input [2]. However, proxy metrics remain limited because they primarily benchmark technical properties of explanations rather than how people interpret, compare, or use them. In particular, they do not capture human responses to presentation format, visual explanations, stakeholder context, or perceived usefulness. As a result, proxy metrics are not suitable to assess the XAI explanation quality in a human-centered way, which is our focus [62]. 2.3 LLMs as Evaluators LLM-based evaluations, often referred to as “LLM-as-a-judge”, have been applied across various tasks, including text summarization, recommendation explanations, and educational feedback [6, 35, 43, 44, 68]. Empirical studies report moderate to strong correlations between LLM-based and human judgments, suggesting that LLMs can approximate human evaluation in many subjective assessment tasks [59, 66, 68]. At the same time, evaluation performance depends on factors such as prompt phrasing and the underlying LLM model, which highlights the importance of standardized and transparent prompting procedures [5, 37]. More broadly, the emerging LLM-as-a-judge paradigm investigates whether LLMs can approximate human judgments or serve as scalable evaluators for complex outputs [5, 16, 26]. However, this literature has not focused on the evaluation of XAI explanation quality. A related but distinct line of work uses LLMs to generate or verbalize model explanations in natural language, for example, through interactive explanation systems (i.e., “talk to the model” [38]). In contrast, our work uses LLMs to evaluate explanations generated by external XAI methods. text:
De oorlog in Oekraïne: de prijs van wegkijken. 👇

Het is veelzeggend wanneer extreemrechts begrip toont voor Poetin omdat brandstof duurder wordt en defensie geld kost. De eigen portemonnee lijkt plots belangrijker dan de vrijheid van een volk dat weigert zich aan het Kremlin te onderwerpen. Achter het discours over besparingen schuilt een ongemakkelijke vraag: hoeveel vrijheid van anderen is men bereid op te offeren om zelf geen offers te hoeven brengen?

De stijgende brandstofprijzen worden mede beïnvloed door de oorlog rond Iran, de dreiging voor de scheepvaart door de Straat van Hormuz en de onzekerheid over de olieaanvoer. Maar wie zich blindstaart op de prijs aan de pomp en tegelijk de Russische agressie relativeert, verliest de werkelijke inzet uit het oog: de veiligheid van heel Europa.

Oekraïne kent een lange geschiedenis van overheersing, onderdrukking en verzet. De Holodomor, de hongersnood onder het Sovjetregime, liet diepe sporen na. Sinds de onafhankelijkheid in 1991 vecht het land voor het recht zijn eigen toekomst te bepalen. Met de annexatie van de Krim in 2014 en de grootschalige invasie van 2022 heeft Rusland dat recht met geweld aangevallen.

Daarbij zijn de persoonlijke aanvallen op president Zelensky bijzonder schrijnend. Hem kleineren, zijn legitimiteit zonder ernstige onderbouwing in twijfel trekken en de verantwoordelijkheid voor de oorlog bij Oekraïne zelf leggen, komt vaak neer op het kritiekloos overnemen van Kremlin-narratieven. Zo wordt de werkelijkheid omgekeerd: de leider van het aangevallen land wordt geviseerd, terwijl de agressor ruimte krijgt om zijn oorlog te rechtvaardigen.

Wanneer Kremlinpropaganda wordt nagepraat om een egoïstische houding tegenover Oekraïne te vergoelijken, is dat meer dan politieke gemakzucht: het vertroebelt bewust of onbewust het onderscheid tussen agressor en slachtoffer.
Kritiek op Zelensky of op het Oekraïense beleid is in een democratie volkomen legitiem. Maar kritiek vergt feiten en nuance, geen slogans die de Russische machtsstrategie in de kaart spelen.

Wie Oekraïne aan zijn lot wil overlaten omdat steun geld kost, vergeet bovendien een fundamenteel principe: agressie die loont, kan verdere agressie aanmoedigen. De rekening van wegkijken kan morgen veel hoger uitvallen, in militaire dreiging, economische ontwrichting, defensiekosten en mensenlevens. De veiligheid van Europa is geen vanzelfsprekendheid die we straffeloos kunnen verwaarlozen.

Natuurlijk mogen energieprijzen, defensiebudgetten en de omvang van onze steun ter discussie staan. Maar ze gebruiken om de onderwerping van Oekraïne te vergoelijken, is geen realisme. Het is een gevaarlijke onderschatting van wat er op het spel staat.

De vrijheid van een volk is geen wisselgeld voor ons comfort. Wie vandaag de agressor napraat om zichzelf geen offers te hoeven getroosten, moet zich afvragen aan welke kant van de geschiedenis zijn woorden uiteindelijk terechtkomen.

text:
**Dan Patrick (Texas Lieutenant Governor) posted a campaign-style video promoting his “Double Nickel” / “Operation Double Nickel” plan to cut school property taxes.**[](<https://t.co/UGzsHFohrg>)

### Key points from the post and video
- The plan lowers the age for the senior homeowner exemption and school property tax freeze from **65 to 55**.
- At 55, homeowners would get their school taxable values frozen earlier (protecting against rising appraisals) plus the larger senior homestead exemption.
- Patrick argues this saves the average homeowner roughly $10,000–$12,000 over the next decade by locking in values 10 years sooner, and it builds toward eliminating school M&O (maintenance and operations) property taxes for typical homeowners over the next couple of legislative sessions via higher exemptions.
- He jokingly ties it to Denny’s: if the restaurant offers a senior discount at 55, Texas can offer stronger property-tax relief at the same age. The video shows him holding a sign with “65 → 55” and is labeled a political ad for Texans for Dan Patrick.

### Background on the current system and the proposal
Texas currently gives homeowners 65+ (or disabled):
- An extra school homestead exemption (recently raised; combined with the general exemption it has been in the $200,000 range for seniors).
- A school tax ceiling/freeze: the school district portion of the bill is locked at the amount paid in the year they first qualify and generally cannot rise later (even if values or rates go up), unless there are significant improvements.

Patrick’s plan would extend the age threshold to 55, further raise general homestead exemptions (building on recent voter-approved increases), and accelerate relief. Reporting indicates it could cover millions more homeowners (roughly 3+ million of Texas’s ~6 million homeowners) and produce annual savings in the hundreds to around $1,000 range for many 55+, with larger cumulative gains from the earlier freeze. He has framed the cost as manageable (under a few billion per biennium in estimates) given Texas’s budget situation, and he contrasts it with full school-tax elimination proposals that he says would require much higher sales taxes.[](<https://t.co/UEgsJFbBeJ>)

This is a legislative proposal for the next session (not current law). Recent Texas property-tax changes have involved raising homestead exemptions and have been popular with voters. The post comes amid ongoing debate over property-tax relief in Texas, including differences with other approaches (such as those associated with Gov. Greg Abbott). Patrick is up for re-election in November 2026.

Replies under the post include criticism on other issues (e.g., THC policy) and skepticism about past tax-relief promises.

In short, the post is a straightforward political pitch for earlier and broader school property-tax relief via a lower senior age threshold and continued exemption increases.

text:
Process Over Narrative: Letting Positions and Risk Dictate the Book

These past few days have reinforced something simple: open positions should largely determine both overall exposure and how aggressive the book is allowed to be.

Staying disciplined when the feed is uniformly negative is rarely comfortable. In practice though, other people’s views have limited relevance. You’re the one who has to live with the P&L, the drawdowns, and the risk parameters you actually set. Those are the constraints that should drive decisions.

Yesterday produced a few clean contrarian mean-reversion setups on an intraday basis. At the same time, the pharma/biotech exposure has continued to hold up relatively well versus the broader market after months of underperformance (in a narrow-breadth environment). Whether that relative strength persists is another question; for now it has simply been more resilient than pure AI-momentum names.

On that point, extreme positioning in a pure AI-momentum framework has, in my view, offered limited asymmetry over recent months. The narrative was already widely priced, while several other sectors had been left behind for a long time. A pure momentum approach focused on that single theme has generally shown a weaker hit rate over that period. Other areas have, at least so far, displayed more durability. That doesn’t make one style superior; it just suggests the edge available in a crowded narrative can compress.

It helps to separate two broad approaches: traders who mainly express pure momentum, and those who are willing to mix different regimes or instruments. There is no requirement to stay fully invested. Cash is a position, and it can act as a hedge. Other non-AI expressions also exist. In my own book this year I deliberately reduced pure momentum exposure and looked for complementary tools; BRK.B has been one of them, providing a way to stay invested outside the dominant narrative without forcing additional tech beta.

A lot of the debate still mixes two different ideas: the desire (or pressure) to remain invested at all times, versus running a more dynamic process that can size up, size down, or stay flat depending on the setup, the risk parameters, and whether a theme has become overly crowded. They are not the same thing.

TRANSCRIPT
An AI memory aid records the same conversations that can contain sensitive personal information. Amazon says Bee turns conversations into summaries, reminders and action items, and can use connected-app context to draft emails and calendar invitations. It says raw audio is processed in real time and deleted while encrypted transcripts remain under user control. Bee Frontier is available now for $74.99; Eclipse is coming soon from $99.99. Optional Bee Pro costs $11.99 monthly, while basic recaps and fourteen-day memory remain available without it.

When shoppers gather products across stores, compatibility and changing prices can complicate the decision. Google says Universal Cart runs on Gemini models, using reasoning to flag compatibility issues. It brings together products found through Search and Gemini and can consider card benefits and merchant offers. The cart is now available to American users with price-drop and restock notifications. Google previously said agent payments would come later, so this launch does not establish autonomous purchases.

Developers wanting control over a powerful AI model face a substantial hardware requirement for local use. Meta released Muse Spark Open as an open-weight multimodal model for coding and agent workflows. Meta lists 816 billion total parameters, 42 billion active parameters and a one-million-token context window. Its local demonstration used two M5 Ultra Mac Studios with roughly one terabyte of unified memory. The weights are downloadable, but this demonstration should not be mistaken for ordinary laptop requirements.

Outside assessments of AI risks depend on seeing more than a public chatbot. Anthropic says six researchers from the evaluation nonprofit METR have now received company hardware, office space and internal access roughly comparable to its risk-assessment teams. That implements the previously announced access agreement. METR will publish analysis of risks, incidents or practices. Anthropic cannot veto publication, though it can require narrowly defined redactions. This is voluntary company oversight, and findings remain pending.

Business websites face a different challenge when attackers adapt to the replies they receive. Japanese security company Bitforest says it observed AI agents reading server responses and adjusting their next actions during attacks between October ten and fourteen. One campaign lasted nearly eight hours and changed through ten phases. It included rapid scans, vulnerability probes and about 250 repeated login attempts. The report identifies neither live models nor attackers and reports no successful compromise. Bitforest still recommends patching and defenses that examine behavior beyond fixed signatures.

A conversational assistant inside a car needs clear limits on its authority. Rivian already routes spoken requests to vehicle software, using local AI models for some tasks and cloud models for harder questions. It says agents will not control steering or braking. In October thirteen remarks, chief executive RJ Scaringe said Rivian wants to add outside AI products. He gave no launch date and said integration work and coordination are still required.

Using AI for driving puts model development and safety evaluation into the vehicle software process. Volvo says future cars will combine its safety systems with Nvidia AI and accelerated computing, including Hyperion, Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack. The stack includes AI models, datasets and simulation tools alongside conventional software and sensor perception. Volvo expects the first equipped vehicle later this decade but did not identify a model. This is a future vehicle plan, not evidence of fully autonomous driving or demonstrated safety gains.

Building a small community game or poll can begin with a written description rather than a conventional coding project. Bluesky has expanded its AI-powered Attie app beyond creating custom feeds to making websites, quizzes, games, polls and other interactive experiences through natural language. Users can bring their own model or use open-weight options. Creations run on Bluesky’s social protocol, and the company says it can distribute them to its network. Details of feature availability and privacy safeguards still need follow-up.

As AI changes work, Germany’s digital minister wants AI-related revenues to help fund the transition. In an October thirteen interview, Karsten Wildberger backed taxing very high AI revenues to finance workforce transition. DW also reports that the finance minister said the government was examining AI’s effects on public finances and social systems. Wildberger’s position is not an adopted tax or a government bill. No tax terms were disclosed, so its cost and practical effects cannot yet be assessed.

AI in drug research raises questions about validating evidence and overseeing systems that change. European medicines regulators are finalizing a clinical-development AI concept paper for public consultation and preparing machine-learning guidance across the medicines lifecycle. Possible clarification areas include validation, risk categories, transparency, third-party tools and submissions. Notes from the October five meeting describe discussions, with guidance still in preparation. Consultation has not begun, and these notes do not create a new binding requirement.

Teachers searching records and drafting paperwork handle information that needs controlled access. Ibaraki City and NTT West are piloting NTT’s tsuzumi two language model for school-document search, summaries, chat questions and drafting. The partners describe local operation and access controls intended to assess safety and usefulness. The pilot began October thirteen in selected municipal schools and runs through March 31, 2027. Surveys and interviews will measure search and writing time, usefulness and usability; no measured savings or classroom results are reported yet.
