text:
Tonbo Imaging IPO: great tech, rich price, rough year. Full breakdown 👇

The issue:
→ Opens Oct 15, closes Oct 19, lists Oct 23
→ Price band ₹665-700, lot of 21 shares (₹14,700)
→ Size ₹852 Cr, 100% Offer for Sale. Zero rupees go to the company
→ At ₹700, market cap is about ₹4,010 Cr
→ Anchors put in ₹255 Cr on Oct 14
→ ~5.5x subscribed by Day 2, GMP around ₹500 (unofficial)

What Tonbo does:
Bengaluru defence electronics OEM. Thermal imagers, weapon sights, targeting systems, missile seekers. 28,000+ systems deployed across 24 countries. About 94% of India's thermal imaging exports by units (FY24-26). Own IP, ITAR-free.

Why people like it:
→ EBITDA margin ~29% in FY26, rare for hardware
→ Order book ₹314 Cr (₹232 Cr domestic, ₹82 Cr overseas)
→ Domestic revenue more than doubled to ₹337 Cr (+115%)
→ Defence indigenisation tailwind
→ HBL Engineering owns 14.25%, so there is a listed way to track it

Why I'm cautious:
→ FY26 revenue down 22.7% to ₹363 Cr, PAT down 30% to ₹51 Cr
→ Exports fell from ₹307 Cr (65% of sales) to ₹20 Cr (5.6%)
→ Q1 FY27: revenue ₹36 Cr, loss of ₹17.7 Cr
→ ~79x FY26 earnings after a down year
→ Operating cash flow negative two years running: -₹136 Cr (FY25), -₹63 Cr (FY26)
→ Top 5 customers were 53% of FY26 revenue and 92% in Q1 FY27
→ 79% of FY26 revenue landed in H2. Tender-driven and lumpy
→ Order book is only 0.87x FY26 revenue

Who's selling:
→ Promoters Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D'Souza sell 19.6 lakh shares. Their stake falls from 17.4% to about 14%
→ The real sellers are the CEAQ entities, about 75% of the offer. CEAQ India exits fully. CEAQ Singapore drops from 25.5% to about 18.2%
→ Their weighted average cost per share (per DRHP): ₹4.83 for India, ₹9.13 for Singapore. Offer price is ₹700
→ Arvind's cost is nil. Ankit and Cecilia's is ₹33.91
→ OFS shrank from 1.81 Cr shares in the DRHP to 1.22 Cr

My take:
This is a bet on order conversion, not on trailing numbers. A 70% GMP means the good news is already in the price. Q2 and Q3 execution decides whether 79x looks cheap or crazy.

Early investors are exiting at 77x to 145x their cost. You are paying 79x earnings for it. Watch the next two quarters, not the GMP.

Not investment advice. @_beingsandip.

beyond ordinary appetite. The animal might be eaten within the gates, but its blood was not available for unrestricted consumption. The LORD had established that boundary. When God granted permission concerning the flesh, the permission did not silently erase His commandment concerning the blood. Biblical liberty operates within what God permits, not within whatever man manages to justify.

The doctrine of the firstborn also finds a greater fulfillment of divine purpose in Jesus Christ, though the scriptural distinctions must remain precise. Christ is called “the firstborn from the dead” in Colossians 1:18, and Romans 8:29 speaks of Him as “the firstborn among many brethren.” First Corinthians 15:20 declares, “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” These passages magnify His preeminence and resurrection victory; they do not mean the eternal Son of God was a created being or merely another member of fallen humanity. Nor do they turn every detail of Israel's firstling legislation into a direct prophecy. The legitimate connection is that the LORD's claims upon the firstborn belong within a biblical pattern that directs attention toward redemption and the supremacy of Christ. Israel's firstlings belonged to God by divine appointment; Jesus Christ stands above all as the sinless Redeemer, risen Lord, and preeminent Head of His Church.
Conclusion
Deuteronomy 15:19–23 teaches Israel that the firstling belonged to the LORD, and belonging to Him carried practical consequences. The firstborn male from the herd or flock was to be sanctified according to God's command. The bullock could not be used for ordinary work. The sheep could not be shorn for ordinary profit. The appointed worship arrangement governed the firstling's presentation and use. A blemished animal could not be offered upon the altar, though God permitted it to be eaten within the gates. Even then, the blood remained prohibited. These are not disconnected regulations scattered across five verses. They reveal a consistent truth: the LORD possesses authority to establish the purpose, condition, treatment, and permitted use of what He has reserved. What God declares holy does not become common merely because man discovers a profitable use for it. The sacred belongs to the One who sanctified it, not to the man who thinks he has found a better arrangement.
The Christian today must understand this passage without attempting to rebuild Israel's sacrificial system. We are not required to consecrate firstborn livestock, sacrifice animals, or observe Mosaic regulations concerning the firstlings. Christ has accomplished the redemption toward which the sacrificial system pointed. Hebrews 10:4 says, “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.” Our salvation rests upon the precious blood of Jesus Christ and His finished work, not upon obedience to the ceremonial law. Yet the New Testament does call redeemed believers to present themselves unto God. Romans 12:1 says, “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” That is not an instruction to return to Moses; it is an appeal grounded in the mercies of God. We do not give ourselves to Christ in order to purchase redemption. We belong to Him because He purchased us, and willing service is a fitting response to a redemption already accomplished.
The searching question, then, is whether we recognize the difference between what God has authorized and what personal advantage would prefer. Israel's farmer might have seen a strong bullock and imagined another profitable season of labor. He might have looked at a healthy sheep and calculated the value of its wool. But the LORD had already spoken concerning both animals. The farmer's arithmetic did not outrank the commandment. Christians face their own temptations to convert ministry into merchandise, spiritual responsibility into personal

Trump rules out nuclear strikes on Iran but threatens further attacks on 'underground nuclear site'
——
US President Donald Trump ruled out using nuclear weapons against the Islamic Republic, while threatening further strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities, including a suspected underground site known as Pickaxe Mountain (Kolang Kouh).

Speaking to Newsmax on Thursday, Trump said Washington did not need nuclear weapons, describing the "mother of all bombs" as a conventional weapon. Asked whether he would deploy US ground troops to attack the suspected facility, he replied that he did not foresee such an operation.

"We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said, warning that Washington might have to launch further military operations if it could not ensure Iran would never acquire one. Despite the Trump administration, and previous US administrations, accusing Iran of intentions to possess or manufacture nuclear weapons, there has been no evidence that prove any such intentions.

Trump also claimed that the war would end "very soon" and that Iranian officials had asked Washington to halt military operations while negotiations continued. He offered no evidence for the claim that Tehran had made such a request. Asked whether he trusted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Trump replied, "I don't trust anybody."

text:
In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed. Its assets were divided among the newly independent states. Ukraine inherited a great deal.

Missiles, nuclear warheads, warships, tanks… and 19 Tu-160 strategic bombers.

You may never have heard of this aircraft. But the Soviets gave it a name: THE WHITE SWAN.

The Tu-160 was one of the most expensive and technologically advanced military aircraft ever built by the Soviet Union. It was among the fastest bombers in the world, capable of carrying nuclear weapons and traveling enormous distances.

That year, Ukraine became the country with the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal.

Almost overnight.

But there was one problem: the launch codes for the nuclear missiles were in Moscow. Ukraine had inherited an enormous arsenal of weapons, but it did not hold the keys to the kingdom.

The 19 White Swans sat motionless at Priluki Air Base.

They could not be used operationally, and their maintenance alone cost millions of dollars every year.

Meanwhile, Ukraine was struggling economically. It had accumulated a massive debt to Russia for natural gas and could not afford to pay it back.

What happened next was more absurd than anything you could invent in a novel.

THE FIRST OFFER: RUSSIA WANTS THE AIRCRAFT

Russia had only six Tu-160 bombers left and urgently needed more.

So it approached Ukraine with an offer:

“Sell us the aircraft. We’ll write off your natural gas debt in return.”

Ukraine was open to the idea, but the two sides had to agree on a price.

Russia offered $25 million per aircraft.

Ukraine said the price was too low.

Negotiations continued for nearly a decade, but no agreement was reached.

Then something unexpected happened.

AN AMERICAN COMPANY ENTERS THE PICTURE

An American private company called Platforms International Corp secretly approached Ukraine.

Its proposal was simple:

“Sell us three Tu-160s. We’ll pay $20 million for all three.”

That’s $20 million in total. Three aircraft. Less than $7 million per plane.

Russia must have been furious when it heard about the deal.

But what did this American company intend to do with these enormous bombers?

TURNING A BOMBER INTO A SATELLITE LAUNCH PLATFORM

The plan was to convert the Tu-160s into airborne satellite launch platforms.

Flying at an altitude of approximately 13,500 meters and at Mach 1.7, the White Swan would release a Pegasus rocket in midair. The rocket would then carry a satellite into orbit.

Technically, the concept was feasible. Ukraine’s cabinet had even approved the plan.

But the U.S. government was alarmed.

Wait a minute. An American private company was trying to buy Soviet strategic bombers while the American government was spending money to destroy those very aircraft!

Washington was running the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction Program, which provided funding to help former Soviet states dismantle nuclear weapons and the systems designed to deliver them.

The underlying principle was straightforward: these weapons should not remain operational or fall into the wrong hands.

The result was deeply ironic.

On one side, an American private company was trying to purchase Soviet bombers. On the other, the U.S. government was paying to have Soviet bombers destroyed.

Two American operations were working in completely opposite directions.

Eventually, pressure from the U.S. government forced the private purchase deal to collapse.

Washington had blocked the American buyer, while Russia, growing impatient, accelerated its negotiations with Ukraine.

A diesel offer may also pressure Ukraine policy.

Ryan McBeth’s geopolitical interpretation is that the diesel proposal may serve two agendas at once. Trump may view additional Russian supply as a way to reduce global diesel prices before the midterm elections. Putin, McBeth argues, may see the offer as leverage over U.S. policy toward Ukraine.

The possible mechanism is political as much as commercial. If Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries are associated with disrupted exports or higher fuel prices, Washington could face pressure to discourage those attacks. Putin might then trade limited energy revenue—or the promise of more supply—for reduced U.S. support for Kyiv.

McBeth also suggests that this pressure could extend to intelligence sharing if Ukraine continues attacking Russian refineries. In that reading, the diesel offer would not simply address fuel markets; it could encourage Trump to distance U.S. policy from Ukraine’s military actions.

McBeth presents this as an inference, not confirmed evidence. The proposal could also reflect commercial motives, efforts to normalize Russian energy exports, or negotiations unrelated to Ukraine. But the strategic possibility matters because a shipment described as an energy measure could influence how Washington weighs support for Kyiv.

The key question is whether the fuel offer changes policy, not merely whether deliveries occur. If Russian diesel arrives without any shift in U.S. support for Ukraine, the leverage theory would become harder to sustain.

Would a diesel offer still give Putin leverage if U.S. support for Ukraine does not change?

text:
🌍 GLOBAL MARKET RECAP — OCTOBER 16, 2026
Hot Inflation, Falling Yields Edition | Updated around 08:45 CEST

Producer prices jumped 6.3%, the fastest pace since 2022, and Treasury yields still fell. The Dow gained 1.1%, Asia rebounded, and Indonesia collapsed 11% on an MSCI warning. When bonds ignore inflation, they are worried about something else.

📜 ON THIS DAY — October 16, 1987
Thirty-nine years ago today, the Dow Jones fell 108 points, about 4.6%. It was the first 100-point drop in its history. In London, the Great Storm had flattened trees and cut power overnight, and most of the City could not get to work. Investors went into the weekend with a weak dollar, a widening trade deficit and the 10-year yield above 10%. On Monday, October 19, the Dow lost 22.6% in a single session: Black Monday. The lesson was not that Friday predicts Monday. It was that markets can carry stress for weeks before liquidity suddenly decides the price. This week, Seoul and Jakarta have offered a smaller reminder of the same rule.

1️⃣ GLOBAL EQUITIES — HOT DATA, BROAD RALLY, TECH LEFT BEHIND
Wall Street closed higher on Thursday despite another hot inflation print, but the leadership changed completely. The S&P 500 rose 0.33% to 7,744, the Dow gained 1.08% to 52,178 and the Russell 2000 jumped 1.38%, while the Nasdaq Composite managed only 0.08% to 26,713 after falling as much as 1.5% in the morning. About seven in ten S&P 500 stocks advanced and eight of eleven sectors finished higher, led by health care, materials and consumer discretionary. Technology fell 0.65% and energy 1.58%. Nvidia lost 1.8%, AMD 1.5% and the TSMC ADR 1.8%. CoreWeave delivered the session's most telling move: down 9.5% in the morning, it closed up 5.9%. Money did not leave equities; it rotated out of the AI trade into the rest of the market.

2️⃣ U.S. MACRO — THE PIPELINE IS FULL OF INFLATION
September producer prices rose 1.3% on the month, more than double the 0.6% forecast, and 6.3% on the year against 5.5% expected: the largest annual increase since 2022. Gasoline prices at the producer level rose more than 20% in a single month. The narrower core measure, excluding food, energy and trade services, rose 0.5% on the month and 5.0% on the year. Following Wednesday's 3.7% CPI, the message is consistent: energy costs from the Gulf war are moving through the supply chain, and part of that will reach consumer prices in the coming months. Today's calendar brings import prices and industrial production, along with Friday options expiry.

3️⃣ BONDS & FED — THE MARKET IS BETTING ON PATIENCE, NOT ON INFLATION
The most important move of the day came from bonds. Instead of rising on the hot PPI, the 10-year Treasury yield fell about 9 basis points to 5.10%, after touching 5.04% intraday, its lowest since late September. The 2-year fell to 4.77%. Two forces explain it. First, Fed officials Michelle Bowman and Mary Daly signalled no rush to tighten, and New York Fed President John Williams said he sees no reason so far to do more than one further hike. Second, investors bought Treasuries as a refuge from stress in AI credit. The odds of a hike on October 28, which approached 50% after CPI, fell to around 25–30%. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh added that AI could bring large economic benefits. The dollar index slipped about 0.5% to around 102.

4️⃣ EUROPE & FX — ERICSSON LEADS, BONDS RALLY
European stocks extended their gains. The Stoxx 600 rose 0.4% to 640.16, its highest close since September 22, with London, Zurich and Paris outperforming Milan and Madrid. Ericsson jumped almost 12% after stronger-than-expected third-quarter sales, while chipmakers and AI infrastructure names such as ASML, Infineon, STMicroelectronics and Schneider Electric lagged. Sovereign bonds rallied with Treasuries: the German 10-year yield fell 5.3 basis points to 3.41%, the French OAT 8.5 basis points to 4.80% and the UK 10-year gilt 5.4 basis points to 5.37%. On the data side, French inflation jumped to 3.4% from 2.6%, eurozone industrial production fell 0.5% in August and the UK economy grew only 0.1%. The euro trades around $1.123 and the yen near 157.8 per dollar.

5️⃣ ASIA — SEOUL REBOUNDS, JAKARTA SUFFERS ITS WORST DAY SINCE 1998
After Thursday's "Black Thursday", Asia found its footing. The Kospi rebounded by around 3–4% in afternoon trade, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix up roughly 4%, although the index remains on track for its worst week in 18 years and foreign investors are still selling. The Nikkei gained about 1.9% to around 65,660, Hong Kong 1.2% and Shanghai 1%, while Taiwan rose only 0.6%. The real shock came from Indonesia: the Jakarta market fell around 11%, its worst session since January 1998, after MSCI flagged a possible downgrade to "standalone" status, below frontier markets. Trading was halted for 30 minutes at the open, the three largest banks fell almost 15% and the rupiah weakened to about 18,070 per dollar, close to its record low. Jakarta is down almost 40% this year, the worst equity market in the world.

6️⃣ OIL, GOLD & COMMODITIES — OIL HOLDS ITS WAR PREMIUM
Brent trades around $105.5 per barrel and WTI around $97.4, slightly lower this morning but heading for a weekly gain. On Thursday WTI rallied about 3% after U.S. crude inventories fell by 8.6 million barrels. Physical supply remains the problem: according to Kpler, flows through Hormuz averaged 11.6 million barrels a day in the week to October 13, against a pre-war baseline of about 17.2 million. The IEA is releasing the remaining 100 million barrels of its emergency stock plan, and Washington is considering easing sanctions on some "shadow fleet" tankers, but ING notes that the risk premium is unlikely to fade without a U.S.–Iran agreement. Before the war, Brent traded around $72. Gold rebounded on Thursday with falling yields, with futures up 1.6% near $4,172, and spot trades around $4,154 this morning. Copper is steady near $14,350 per tonne.

7️⃣ GEOPOLITICS — THE GULF WAR IS SPREADING ACROSS THE ARABIAN PENINSULA
At least ten ships have been hit around Hormuz since Sunday, the highest number for any comparable period since the conflict began. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claim a container ship sank after hitting a mine south of the Strait; this has not been independently verified. Tehran says the Strait is "closed", while U.S. Central Command says it still moves millions of barrels a day. Washington announced new sanctions on financial networks linked to Iran. On the Saudi front, the Houthis have targeted Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport 20 times since October 1, and the EU–GCC summit scheduled for October 24 in Riyadh has been postponed. The IMF now expects the Middle East and Central Asia region to contract by 0.3% this year. For markets, the war is no longer just an oil story; it is a growth story for the whole Gulf.

8️⃣ ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE — THE STRESS HAS MOVED FROM STOCKS TO CREDIT
The AI trade is now being priced in the credit market. CoreWeave's bonds traded at yields above 15% and its credit default swaps hit record levels intraday, before the shares recovered. The company carries around $48 billion of debt. SoftBank's five-year CDS widened 24 basis points in one day to about 424, and Oracle's widened to roughly 288. Hyperscalers including Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle have issued more than $228 billion of bonds so far this year, more than twice their 2025 total. This is the paradox of the moment: government yields are falling, but borrowing costs for the weaker AI borrowers are rising. That gap is what bond investors are telling us.

9️⃣ CRYPTO — BITCOIN SWEEPS $80K AND BUYERS STEP IN
Bitcoin briefly broke below $80K on Thursday afternoon, touching about $79.8K, then recovered quickly to $82.5K. It trades around $82K this morning, up about 0.7% in 24 hours. Ether is around $2,435 and Solana near $105. Spot Bitcoin ETFs were almost flat on Thursday, with net inflows of about $5 million, after outflows of $261 million on Wednesday; October flows are still negative by about $540 million. A quick sweep below $80K that is bought back is exactly the constructive signal I described in yesterday's My 2 Cents. The confirmation is still missing: a daily close above $82.8K, and then a reclaim of the $83.7K kijun. A daily close below $80.1K would cancel the signal. For long-term accumulation, BTC, ETH and SOL should continue to be assessed through disciplined DCA, separately from speculative trading.

🔟 MARKET STRUCTURE — WHEN BONDS IGNORE INFLATION, LISTEN TO THE BONDS
Hot inflation and falling yields on the same day is not a contradiction; it is information. The bond market is saying that slower growth and credit risk worry it more than producer prices, and that the Fed will wait rather than tighten into stress. Equities agreed: money left AI and moved into small caps, health care, materials and financials.

The principal transmission chain remains Energy → Inflation → Fed Expectations → Front-End Yields → Dollar → Risk Assets → Crypto. This week a second chain dominates: AI Debt → Credit Spreads → Flight to Treasuries → Rotation out of Tech. Indonesia adds a third: Market Access → Passive Outflows → Emerging-Market Contagion.

Today I am monitoring the U.S. 10-year between 5.00% and 5.20%, October hike odds near 25–30%, CoreWeave and Oracle credit spreads, the rupiah near its record low, Brent between $100 and $108, and Bitcoin's daily close relative to $82.8K.

Constructive scenario: yields keep falling without a growth scare, AI credit stabilises and the rotation broadens. In that case the S&P 500 could retest its highs, Asian chips could extend the rebound and Bitcoin could reclaim $83.7K.

Negative scenario: a new spike in AI credit spreads, contagion from Jakarta to other emerging markets and an oil shock from Hormuz. Under those conditions the falling yields would stop being a relief and start being a warning.

What would invalidate my cautious view: a clear tightening in AI credit spreads together with stable oil, which would show that this week was a positioning flush rather than a funding problem.

In 1987 the warning came on Friday and the crash on Monday. In 2026 the warnings are coming from the bond market every day. The question is whether anyone is listening.

Are falling yields good news for risk assets, or a warning sign? 👇

text:
Some consequences stand out if Le Pen wins:

1) NATO: France would stay a member but become less reliable. Macron's offer of a European dimension to French nuclear deterrence would likely end. 

2) Ukraine: France would move from being a co-leader to being a brake.

3) EU: veto-player at a critical moment. She no longer advocates Frexit or leaving the euro. Instead, she favours a constitutional push to make French law take primacy over EU law. 

4) Defence-industrial policy: "strategic autonomy" would turn national. The National Rally supports higher defence spending, but through French sovereign industry, not Commission-led instruments. The paradox is that Europe would get more French defence capability but less European defence integration.

5) JEF would become a hedge against France as well as the US. The ten members (the UK, the Nordics, the Baltics and the Netherlands) already value it as a fast, flexible format that isn't hostage to unanimity in Brussels or Washington. With Paris unreliable on Ukraine and deterrence, northern Europe would lean on it harder.

6) Britain's pivot partner would weaken. The UK runs a two-track European defence strategy: JEF in the north, France for high-end capability and the nuclear dimension. Several UK-France arrangements would be at risk. 

7) France's own competing format to JEF would wither. The French-led European Intervention Initiative (EI2) overlaps heavily with JEF membership. Under Le Pen, it would likely lose political drive. That would remove one of Paris's main channels into northern European security thinking, leaving JEF largely unrivalled.

8) The Franco-German axis would shift toward Berlin–London. With France turning inward, Germany would become the natural continental anchor.

Pope Paul VI was the first pope ever to visit America. U.S. President Johnson ("protestant," 1st degree Freemason, dropout of Jesuit Georgetown University Law School) sought Paul VI's wisdom in an unannounced meeting to help end the Vietnam War. Francis Rooney’s, who served as U.S. Ambassador to the Holy See under George W. Bush (2005–2008), book The Global Vatican reveals this.

Pope Paul VI landed at Kennedy Airport on October 4, 1965. He gave his “No more war!” speech at the UN, met Johnson for 45 minutes at the Waldorf Astoria, said mass at Yankee Stadium, and was gone in under 14 hours.

New York all but bowed to the pope's presence: schools and stores closed, millions lined the motorcade route, and ninety thousand filled Yankee Stadium for mass. Fourteen hours later the pope was gone, leaving the city “breathless and amazed.” Even Washington felt it, Times columnist James Reston wrote that after so much talk of war, the pope’s simple call for peace was “almost startling.”

On December 23, 1967, flying home from Australia and a stop with troops in Vietnam, U.S. President Johnson “landed, unannounced, in Rome.” The meeting was “hastily arranged,” and many of his own advisors weren’t told until they were airborne. He helicoptered into the Vatican gardens to avoid war protesters (the helicopter sank into soft ground on landing), and sat down with the pope just before 9 p.m.

Johnson and his advisors, “with options few and dwindling,” “turned to the pope for help.” His two requests: a Vatican representative to visit American POWs in North Vietnam, and — “clearly the main reason for the visit” — the pope’s help getting South Vietnam and the Viet Cong into informal talks. Paul VI pushed back on the bombing (“The Church cannot give its approval to bombing as a means of defending liberty”) and offered to be an intermediary. The meeting ended with Johnson gifting the pope a bust of himself.

text:
🇺🇸 TRUMP SAYS ZELENSKY DOESN'T WANT PEACE AND SUGGESTS A DEAL WITH RUSSIA WITHOUT HIM

On October 15, Donald Trump launched another attack on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, accusing him of refusing to negotiate peace, condemning Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, and suggesting that any eventual agreement with Moscow would be reached without Ukraine's current president.

Speaking to Newsmax host Rob Finnerty at the White House, Trump confirmed that he had personally demanded that Zelensky stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure.

"Zelensky is not the person we should be dealing with. Biden gave him hundreds of billions of dollars," Trump declared.

Asked whether he had lost confidence in Zelensky, Trump replied: "He doesn't want to make a deal. He says he wants to make a deal, but he doesn't. I'm not a big fan of Zelensky."

Trump went further, suggesting that peace negotiations might proceed without Ukraine's elected leader. He offered no explanation of how such an arrangement would work or whether Washington intended to pressure Kyiv into changing its government.

"I find Zelensky much harder to deal with than Putin," Trump admitted.

The American president then attacked Ukraine for resuming strikes against Russian oil refineries, claiming they were driving up global fuel prices.

"I want Zelensky to stop, and I want Putin to stop. If Zelensky is hitting oil refineries again, all he's doing is driving up global oil prices. I think it's a disgrace. There are plenty of other targets."

Trump specifically complained that Russian refineries produce diesel fuel needed by the United States and the rest of the world.

These remarks followed reports of a Ukrainian strike on a Rosneft refinery in Russia's Ryazan region on October 15, which reportedly caused a fire.

The controversy comes amid reports of a proposed arrangement between Trump and Putin concerning Russian diesel supplies and the easing of American sanctions restrictions.

Trump also questioned how long Zelensky had remained in office.

"Frankly, I think Zelensky has been there far too long," he said, supporting the idea of Ukrainian presidential elections despite the ongoing war.

He then cited an unidentified Ukrainian woman's interview, claiming she had blamed Zelensky for the destruction of Ukraine and the deaths and injuries of Ukrainian soldiers. Trump provided no information allowing her identity or statements to be independently verified.

Discussing Russia's enormous manpower advantage, Trump declared: "Russia is a huge country, and it can lose a million men, and there will still be millions more behind them. Ukraine doesn't have that kind of manpower."

Meanwhile, the attempted energy ceasefire has collapsed. Trump announced an agreement on October 11, but Zelensky reported renewed Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure the following day.

Zelensky made Ukraine's position clear: Russia must stop attacking Ukrainian power stations, critical infrastructure, and civilians if it wants Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil facilities.

On October 15, Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian refineries, arguing that Moscow had failed to honor the proposed ceasefire.

Zelensky also warned in an interview with Piers Morgan that Ukraine was losing the United States as a strong partner.

Now Trump is openly linking Ukraine's refusal to abandon strikes against Russia's oil industry with Zelensky's political future and participation in peace negotiations.

The White House has not formally suspended contacts with Kyiv, but the possibility of further restrictions on American assistance remains an increasingly serious concern.

Russia invaded Ukraine. Russia destroys Ukrainian cities. Russia kills Ukrainian civilians. Yet Trump repeatedly directs his anger at the country defending itself rather than the aggressor.

And all of this is unfolding before our eyes, almost live on television.

text:
There is something deeply frustrating about waking up every morning feeling as though you’ve just run a marathon, when all you’ve done is sleep.

For most people, sleeping means resting, recovering, and starting over. For me, not even the night offers a moment of respite.

My autonomic nervous system doesn’t function properly. My body has to make a constant effort to regulate functions that should happen automatically, without me ever having to think about them. And that effort continues even while I’m asleep.

Garmin calls it “stress.” But what those graphs show, in my case, isn’t simply psychological stress. It’s an estimate of the physiological strain my body is under.

This morning, I woke up with a Body Battery of 27 out of 100. The day hadn’t even started, and I was already exhausted.

And that’s how it is, day after day.

The most frustrating part is that the world doesn’t stop just because you’re exhausted. You still have to get up, work, concentrate, fulfill your responsibilities, talk to people, and keep going. Do all those things that seem so simple when your body functions the way it should.

Some days I feel angry. Other days, an overwhelming sadness. And on many days, I’m so tired that I don’t even have the energy to get angry.

There’s also the psychological toll of living like this. Of never being able to assume that tomorrow you’ll feel better. Of having to calculate how much energy you can spend on such ordinary things that most people wouldn’t even think twice about. Of wanting to do a thousand things and knowing that your body might not allow you to do even half of them.

And perhaps one of the hardest parts is that, from the outside, nobody can really see what’s happening.

You might see me smiling, working, going out to take photographs, or having a conversation and think I’m fine. What you don’t see is how much effort some of those things take. Or how I feel afterward.

I don’t want to spend my life resting. I want to live it. I want to be able to make plans without first wondering whether I’ll have the strength. I want to wake up one morning and feel like I’ve actually slept.

And above all, I’m tired of being tired.

Because one thing is reaching the end of the day with no energy left after having lived it to the fullest. It’s something entirely different to wake up with no energy at all and have to find a way to live anyway.

text:
When national identity retreats, what fills the space? The panel says fragmentation.

Konstantin Kisin, Francis Foster, Winston Marshall and Tom Slater present a broader theory behind the episode’s discussion of France: Western institutions have weakened national and civic identities without offering a convincing replacement.

Their concern is that people do not stop seeking belonging when national identity is delegitimised. They may instead attach themselves to ethnic, religious, online or ideological communities. Those loyalties can become more powerful precisely because they offer the solidarity and moral purpose that mainstream institutions no longer provide. The panel rhetorically describes the result as “Lebanonization”—a warning about competing group identities, not an established diagnosis of France or the wider West.

They connect this theory to youth unrest, social-media mobilisation and education that treats history primarily as a struggle between oppressors and victims. In their account, young people can gain status by condemning their own society, while anti-national movements offer both community and a clear moral script. That helps explain why some white French youths may join protests directed against Western institutions: participation can signal virtue and supply belonging.

The argument matters because it shifts the policy question. Instead of asking only how to suppress disorder, it asks what positive identity could make pluralistic societies cohesive. The panel’s answer is a civic nationalism grounded in shared participation rather than ancestry.

What kind of civic identity could unite people without demanding cultural uniformity?

What do you make of this point?

text:
Do you ever wonder why many Jews do not accept Jesus Christ as the Messiah???

To understand why the vast majority of Jewish people do not accept Jesus as the Messiah, it helps to look at how the Jewish definition of the Messiah differs fundamentally from the Christian definition.

While the creation of modern Israel in 1948 is a massive milestone in Jewish history, the theological reasons for not believing in Jesus actually go back thousands of years to ancient Biblical texts.

Here is why Judaism and belief in Jesus diverged:

1. Different Expectations of the Messiah

In the Hebrew Bible (the Old Testament), the Messiah is described as a human king, a descendant of King David, who will achieve specific, physical goals on Earth during his lifetime. In Judaism, Jesus is not seen as fulfilling these prophecies, which include:
•Universal Peace: Building a world without war or weapons.
•The Ingathering of Exiles: Bringing all Jewish people back to the land of Israel.
•The Third Temple: Rebuilding the Holy Temple in Jerusalem.
•Universal Knowledge: Creating a world where everyone automatically knows and worships God.
Because Jesus's ministry did not result in these global changes during his lifetime, Jewish theology concludes that he was not the promised Messiah.

2. The Concept of God

Judaism is strictly monotheistic. In Jewish thought, God is a single, indivisible entity who cannot take human form or have physical children. Therefore, the Christian concepts of the Trinity (God existing in three persons) and the idea of Jesus as both God and man contradict foundational Jewish beliefs about the nature of God.

3. Salvation and Sin

In Christianity, the Messiah's primary role is spiritual—dying for humanity's sins to offer salvation and entry into heaven. In Judaism, there is no concept of "original sin" that requires a divine savior. Judaism teaches that every person has a direct relationship with God and can obtain forgiveness for mistakes through sincere prayer, repentance, and doing good deeds, without needing an intermediary.

4. How 1948 Connects to This
The establishment of Israel in 1948 was a political, historical, and national event rather than a miraculous messianic age. While many Jews see the return to the land as a deeply meaningful historical fulfillment, it was achieved through human effort and international diplomacy, rather than by a single messianic ruler bringing about universal world peace.

THE REPLICATOR:
The End of Scarcity: How Matter Itself Might Become Programmable
For generations, stories like Star Trek showed a future where people no longer worked for survival. 
Food, tools, and everyday objects appeared on demand from a wall unit called a replicator. No money changed hands. No one went hungry. 
The idea was simple: 
if matter can be rearranged at will, the old rules of scarcity stop applying.
That vision is still fiction. 
But the underlying idea—building objects atom by atom from basic elements—has a real scientific name and a clear (if still distant) technical path. 
Here is a plain-language version of how that path is sometimes described, along with the two real references often linked to it.
What “Atomic Synthesis” Actually Means:
Everything physical is made of atoms. 
A piece of plastic, a tomato, a cotton shirt, and a steel bolt are just different arrangements of a few common elements—mainly carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen, plus smaller amounts of other atoms.
Atomic synthesis means placing those individual atoms into exactly the positions needed to form a finished object. It is the opposite of today’s manufacturing, which cuts, melts, or molds bulk material.
Scientists can already do tiny versions of this. 
Researchers have used focused laser beams (optical tweezers) to pick up single atoms and bond them into a molecule. 
Other teams use the tip of a scanning probe microscope to move atoms on a surface one by one, or to remove an atom and insert a different one in its place. These experiments prove the principle. 
Scaling the same precision from a few atoms to an apple, a pair of shoes, or a spare part is the enormous engineering gap that remains.
The Salvatore Pais Patents (in simple terms):
In the mid-2010s, aerospace engineer Salvatore Pais filed a series of patent applications while working for the U.S. Navy. 
The patents describe radical machines that, if they worked as claimed, would generate extremely intense electromagnetic fields. 
Proposed uses included:
A craft that reduces its own inertia so it can accelerate or change direction with far less energy.
Devices that produce high-energy electromagnetic fields strong enough, in theory, to affect the vacuum itself.
A compact fusion reactor the size of a vehicle.
Methods claimed to create room-temperature superconductors.
Navy officials supported the patent process, arguing the concepts were “operable” and that competitors (especially China) might be pursuing similar ideas. 
Public reporting later showed the Navy spent roughly half a million dollars testing aspects of the claimed effect and could not confirm it. 
No working prototype of any of these systems has been publicly demonstrated, and most of the patents have since expired or been abandoned. 
They remain speculative proposals rather than proven technology.
The Kwast Doctrine (in simple terms)
Retired U.S. Air Force Lieutenant General Steven Kwast has argued for years that space is the next decisive economic and strategic domain. 
His core points are:
Whoever builds the infrastructure for energy, transport, manufacturing, and communications in the space between Earth and the Moon first will hold long-term advantage.
Space offers essentially unlimited solar energy and access to resources that could change Earth’s economy.
Current military and industrial thinking is still rooted in 20th-century ideas of scarcity and terrestrial logistics; a dedicated Space Force (and civilian counterpart) is needed to develop the new capabilities.
Kwast’s emphasis is on strategy, infrastructure, and economic leadership in space rather than a specific recipe for free energy on Earth. 
The connection sometimes drawn between his ideas and matter-rearrangement technology is interpretive: if abundant clean energy and advanced manufacturing become available in space, the practical barriers to large-scale atomic assembly could shrink.
(Cont’d #2👇)

text:
The Core of the Conflict
Musk has taken a harsh, public stance against California’s laws and school policies regarding children’s gender identity. Specifically, he was incensed by Assembly Bill 1955 (the SAFETY Act), which Governor Newsom signed into law in 2024.
Musk described this as a "mass destruction of parental rights" and "the final straw." He noted that he had warned Newsom a year earlier that such legislation would drive families and companies to leave California to protect their children. This is deeply personal for him: he has stated publicly that his son (now his daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson) was "taken" by gender ideology, and he opposes medical interventions for minors.
Why the Move to Texas (and Why He’s Doing It Despite the High Cost)
The reasons have been building for years:
California’s high taxes (particularly the state income tax, which does not exist in Texas).
Strict business regulations, environmental standards, and the influence of labor unions.
Policies during the COVID-19 pandemic (he famously labeled the forced closure of the Tesla factory "fascist").
Crime rates and the overall quality of life in San Francisco and Los Angeles.
And, on top of all this, the legislation he views as an assault on parental rights.
Tesla relocated its headquarters to Austin in 2021, followed by its legal incorporation. In 2024, Musk announced that the headquarters for both SpaceX and X (formerly Twitter) would also move—to Starbase and Austin, respectively. He himself has lived in Texas for some time.
Admittedly, relocating headquarters and personnel involves immense logistical challenges and significant costs. For Musk, however, this is a matter of the long-term environment: taxes, regulations, and policies affecting families and businesses. Texas offers a more favorable climate—lower taxes, fewer restrictions, and a growing ecosystem (it is already home to dozens of his companies and thousands of his employees). Many other firms are also relocating from California to Texas for the same reasons; this is not just his own personal battle.

CANCELING THE ONES THAT MAKE IT HARD
 
"The gym says I have to cancel in person. I live 300 miles away now."
 
"Then you put it in writing. And you don't let them stall you."
 
Some companies make canceling hard on purpose: hidden buttons, phone-only cancellations, endless "are you sure?" screens.
 
A federal "click to cancel" rule was struck down by a federal appeals court in July 2025, before it took effect. But the law isn't on the companies' side either. A federal law called ROSCA already requires companies selling subscriptions online to give you a simple way to stop the charges. In September 2025, Amazon agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle FTC claims, including that it made Prime hard to cancel.
 
Some states go further. In California, if you signed up online, you have to be able to cancel online. If the company shows you a "stay with us" offer, it has to show a cancel button right next to it.
 
And about that retention offer: when you try to cancel, many services offer a discount to stay. If you actually like the service, take it. If you don't, say no.
 
THE FIX:
1. Look for the cancel option under Account, Membership, Billing or Plan.
2. If you hit a wall, search "[company name] cancel subscription" for the direct path.
3. If they insist on a phone call, say: "I'd like to cancel my membership, effective today. Please send me written confirmation."
4. If they insist on a letter, send it by certified mail with your account number and the date.
5. Hear the retention offer, but only take it if you'd keep the service anyway.
6. Keep every confirmation number, email and screenshot.
 
Companies make it easy to start and hard to stop. Paperwork makes it easy again.

text:
ADAM’S SIN IS NOT YOUR SIN — YOU WERE NOT IN EDEN

Let me say this plainly because this religious tradition has confused many people:
Adam sinned. You did not.
Adam was created, instructed, warned, and presented with a choice. He was in a state of accountability. God gave him a command, and Adam chose against God’s provision of life.
But you were not in Eden.
You did not receive that command.
You did not eat that fruit.
You did not commit Adam’s transgression.
So how did Adam’s personal act become your personal sin?
It didn't.
And if the theology is that every human being already personally committed Adam’s sin simply by being born, then evangelism becomes difficult to explain. Why preach the gospel to someone for a sin they never personally committed?

Look at Abel.
Abel was Adam’s biological son.
Yet Hebrews 11:4 says:
“By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice... by which he obtained witness that he was righteous.”

Righteous?
In the very house of Adam?
And then you have Cain, his brother, who is presented completely differently.
Same father.
Same household.
But different responses.
Abel believed. Cain did not.
So Adam’s transgression did not erase individual accountability.
Adam set a pattern.

Paul says:
“...even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression.”
— Romans 5:14

That phrase should make you pause.
“Had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression.”
Adam was presented with a choice. "life and death" he decided to work away from life(Christ).
And humanity, when it comes to a place of accountability, is likewise confronted with the question of whether we will receive or reject the life God has revealed.
And what is that life?
Christ is life!
Jesus said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
— John 14:6

So the issue is not that you personally committed Adam’s crime.
The issue is what you do when you come to accountability and am confronted with God's truth and His provision of life.
Adam rejected God's command concerning the tree of life. 
And the tree of life is here today (Christ)
If you, at your own point of accountability, reject the life God has revealed in Christ, that is your own response and your own responsibility.

Adam's sin is not your sin.
Adam's choice is not your choice.
But Adam's transgression became a pattern that Scripture uses to explain the entrance and reign of death.

Now before someone jumps into Romans 3:23 screaming, “ALL HAVE SINNED!” 😂
READ THE CONTEXT!
Don't turn one verse into a theological weapon while ignoring the argument Paul is making.
Romans 5:13 says:
“For until the law sin was in the world: but sin is not imputed when there is no law.”
And Romans 7:9 says:
“For I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.”
CONTEXT MATTERS!
The Law exposes and identifies transgression; don't casually turn Paul's discussion of sin, law, death, Adam and accountability into “you personally committed Adam's sin.”
The law declared everyone a sinner not God, and Christ paid for the requirements of the law.

Adam sinned in Adam.
You are accountable for your own response to God.
And this is why the gospel must be preached.
Not to tell people:
“You are guilty because Adam ate.”
But to proclaim:
Christ has come.
Christ is life.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Adam is not the Saviour.
CHRIST IS.
Adam is not the final message.
CHRIST IS.
Death is not the final destination of the gospel.
LIFE IS FOUND IN CHRIST.
So stop making Adam the centre of salvation.
The question is not merely:
“What did Adam do?”
The question is:
“What will you do when you are confronted with the life God has revealed in Christ?”
Because Adam made his choice.
And when you come to accountability, you will make yours.
Christ is life

D.A

text:
Cybernetic (Systems) Analysis: Why They Publicly Announce the ZE PAK–SGE Agreement Despite Private Financing Plans and Delisting
=======================

On 13 October 2026, ZE PAK (controlled by the Solorz family) and SGE (Michał Sołowow’s company) signed a shareholders’ agreement to form a special-purpose vehicle for up to six BWRX-300 small modular reactors (total 1,800 MW) at the Pątnów site — the location of a retiring coal-fired plant near Konin.

Key structure:
SGE** takes the majority stake and contributes exclusive rights to the BWRX-300 technology for the Pątnów area.
ZE PAK** contributes the land (partly as an in-kind contribution, partly sold for up to ~PLN 300 million net, payable 2028–2030) and holds a minority stake with a put option to sell its shares to SGE for €100 million if agreed milestones are met within five years.
ZE PAK has publicly stated that large reactors should remain a state responsibility, while SMRs can be developed by private entities.

In parallel, the Solorz family (via Cypriot vehicle Argumenol) plans a tender offer for the remaining 34% of ZE PAK shares at PLN 18, aiming for delisting from the Warsaw Stock Exchange. SGE itself is raising private equity (recently PLN 500 million from Polish entrepreneurs such as Rafał Brzoska, Michał Brański, ElevenLabs founders and others, plus international capital including GE Vernova; the round is targeting around €800 million). Sołowow has spoken of the overall programme requiring very large private capital (equity first, then debt) rather than state debt, with a possible SGE IPO around 2028.

Why publicise and “boast” about the signatures if the project is meant to be private and largely outside the stock market?

There is no real contradiction. In cybernetic terms (systems, information flows, feedback loops, control and uncertainty reduction), the announcement functions as a steering signal inside a complex system that inevitably interacts with public institutions.

Signalling progress and reducing uncertainty for private capital  
   SGE is actively raising equity from high-net-worth individuals and private investors. A concrete agreement with a site, defined contributions and exit options is a stronger signal than declarations alone. It lowers perceived risk, helps close the current round and supports subsequent rounds. The public announcement is feedback directed at potential capital providers: “We have a location, a land partner, technology rights and a workable structure.” Later project debt or a possible IPO also benefits from a visible track record.

Signalling to the regulatory and political system  
   Even a privately led SMR project requires decisions-in-principle, permits, grid access, potential support mechanisms (e.g. Contracts for Difference or equivalents), environmental approvals and political stability. A public announcement builds a narrative of momentum and private initiative, creating a feedback loop: media coverage → regulators and politicians → greater willingness to engage or lower resistance. In a strategic sector, public information is a tool for managing the surrounding system. Both parties frame the project as a model energy transition (coal-to-nuclear on the same site) and a contribution to energy security.

Value crystallisation for ZE PAK and the logic of delisting  
   The agreement makes the project’s value visible (land contribution + option) before minority shareholders exit. The positive market reaction showed that investors recognised the potential. Delisting removes quarterly reporting pressure, minority-shareholder constraints and short-termism, allowing longer-term private control. ZE PAK extracts value without having to fund the multi-billion construction itself — it contributes land and retains an exit option. The public signal comes first; private control follows.

Social, local and partner acceptance  
   The Konin region is undergoing a coal phase-out. Public communication builds local support, job prospects and acceptance among residents and workers. It also attracts further partners (EPC contractors, industrial offtakers, operators). Sołowow has called Pątnów one of Poland’s most critical energy locations — the announcement is simultaneously a signal to the grid and the broader power system.

Systemic logic and feedback  
   Information as a resource: In a high-complexity system (technology + regulation + capital + society + grid), the absence of public signals increases uncertainty and slows resource flows.  
   Control through signalling: The announcement is not an end in itself; it is a means of influencing the behaviour of the environment (capital arrives, regulators do not block, local communities accept).  
   Optionality: The minority stake + put option structure lets both sides manage risk. Publicity does not mean the construction capital will come from the ZE PAK stock market; it will primarily come from SGE and its private investors, followed by project-level debt.  
   No contradiction with “private”: “Private” mainly means without dominant state equity and without loading the state budget, not “in complete silence.” In nuclear energy, total silence is neither possible nor rational.

Summary: They publicise the agreement because, in a private SMR model, a visible progress signal is one of the key tools for mobilising resources (private equity, later debt, and cooperation with the state as regulator). Delisting ZE PAK enables longer-term control on the Solorz side, while the agreement allows them to capture value with limited capital at risk. This is a classic information game in a high-barrier, high-complexity system — not PR for its own sake, but active management of feedback loops.

(Based on official ZE PAK/SGE communications, current reports and media coverage from October 2026. The situation remains dynamic.)

text:
October 16,1781.

By mid-October 1781, British Lieutenant General Charles Cornwallis found his army of roughly 8,000 troops tightly besieged at Yorktown, Virginia, by a combined American and French force under George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau. Allied artillery had already captured key redoubts and was pounding the British positions relentlessly, while a French naval blockade under Admiral de Grasse prevented any relief by sea. With supplies dwindling, disease spreading, and no realistic hope of timely reinforcement from New York, Cornwallis concluded that remaining in place would only lead to the destruction of his command.

On the night of October 16, he therefore ordered a desperate evacuation across the York River to the British-held post at Gloucester Point. The plan called for ferrying the bulk of his light infantry and other selected units in the available boats under cover of darkness, concentrating enough strength on the Gloucester side to break through the screening forces of French and American troops commanded by the Duc de Lauzun and others, and then marching northward in hopes of eventual junction with British forces farther up the coast. A diversionary sortie was also launched against the allied siege works to distract attention from the river crossing.

The attempt began under difficult conditions, but a sudden and violent storm swept over the area as the boats were shuttling troops. Heavy winds and rough water scattered the vessels, prevented orderly embarkation, and made further crossings impossible. Cornwallis was forced to halt the operation and recall the units already moved or in transit back to the Yorktown side of the river, abandoning the breakout entirely.

With the escape route closed and the allied bombardment resuming at full intensity the next morning, Cornwallis recognized that further resistance offered no prospect of success. On October 17 he sent out a flag of truce seeking a cessation of hostilities and terms of surrender; negotiations followed, and the formal capitulation of the British army at Yorktown and Gloucester took place on October 19, effectively ending major combat in the American Revolutionary War.

The Defector: A Russian Officer Who Betrayed His Country and Helped Ukraine Kill Hundreds

A remarkable—and deeply disturbing—piece of investigative journalism by @mjluxmoore of The Wall Street Journal (@WSJ).

It tells the extraordinary story of Lieutenant Lev Stupnikov, a young Russian officer who secretly supplied Ukrainian intelligence with troop positions, military communications, and operational plans—information used in attacks that reportedly killed more than 300 of his fellow Russian soldiers.

In one particularly devastating strike, 68 Russian servicemen were killed and another 60 wounded, including senior officers whose whereabouts Stupnikov had betrayed.

What makes the account so unsettling is not merely the scale of the destruction, but the extraordinary ease with which a serving officer was able to turn against his own army—and continue doing so while surrounded by men who trusted him.

Stupnikov, increasingly disillusioned with corruption and military life, became one of Ukraine's most effective intelligence assets. Yet behind the remarkable espionage lies a darker story—one of betrayal, calculated killing, and the psychological burden of watching one's own comrades die.

His mother, herself an opponent of Vladimir Putin, would play an unexpected part in his eventual escape.

The article also offers a fascinating glimpse into Ukraine's clandestine intelligence operations, including efforts to recruit Russians willing not merely to oppose the Kremlin, but to take up arms against it.

There is, of course, a profound moral question running through this extraordinary account.

Is Stupnikov a courageous dissident who turned against an unjust war—or a military officer who betrayed the men serving beside him and knowingly sent hundreds to their deaths?

The distinction depends, perhaps, upon which side of the battlefield one happens to be standing.

An exceptional piece of reporting—and a chilling reminder that, in war, the enemy is not always across the front line.

Protests are democratic; coercion and chaos are not. The government must distinguish dissent from disruption, and protesters must understand that democracy offers a ballot box, not a shortcut to power.

text:
The IEA's diesel announcement is welcome news if you're buying fuel for a fleet. It still doesn't tell you what your supplier will charge for next week's delivery.

On October 15, IEA member countries agreed to speed up the remaining releases under their March emergency action, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel.

The announcement gives a total volume. It doesn't give every buyer a loading date.

Member countries have to carry out the releases through their own stockholding systems. The fuel is held in different places, under different arrangements, so there isn't one timetable for getting all of it into commercial use.

Some reserves are already stored in facilities that serve the normal fuel trade. France's SAGESS, for example, uses third-party terminals and refineries, with access to existing distribution networks. Those barrels don't necessarily need a long sea voyage before a buyer can use them.

Elsewhere, a buyer may need a coastal shipment, a barge booking or space in a pipeline. A terminal with fuel available nearby is a very different proposition from a cargo that still needs to be loaded overseas.

The release process varies too. Germany's reserve agency generally offers released volumes to member companies in weekly portions over four weeks. That tells you something about how the stock becomes available. It doesn't mean every customer receives cheaper diesel four weeks after the IEA announcement.

Fuel specifications also have to match the market where it will be sold. But emergency stocks are managed and checked for quality. We shouldn't assume all stored diesel needs fresh treatment for winter before anyone can lift it.

Prices can move ahead of the physical deliveries. A supplier expecting more competition may lower its quote before the extra fuel arrives. A buyer facing a local shortage may see much less improvement, especially if transport remains expensive.

Then there is the bill the customer actually pays.

A fleet buying diesel directly is watching its supplier's price. A retailer paying a carrier's fuel surcharge may be looking at a different number altogether. UPS's U.S. ground surcharge, for example, adjusts weekly using a published diesel index. A cheaper wholesale cargo doesn't immediately change that calculation.

Pipeline tariffs, terminal charges and delivery costs also remain part of the delivered price. They don't all fall alongside the fuel itself.

The release can help without helping every buyer at the same time. A fleet still has trucks to fuel this week. Until its supplier offers a better delivered price and a loading date it can use, it has to budget for the fuel actually available to it.

🌴 THE VICE FILES | EPISODE 3 🌴

Miami Vice: Cool Runnin’ (1984)

Season/Episode: S1.E3
Original Airdate: October 5, 1984
Director: Lee H. Katzin
Writer: Joel Surnow

Welcome back to Miami, pal. This time, the streets are heating up, and the Noogman is about to make his entrance!

Sonny Crockett (Don Johnson) and Ricardo Tubbs (Philip Michael Thomas) are investigating a violent Jamaican drug gang responsible for a series of deadly robberies targeting Miami’s drug dealers.

The case takes a tragic turn when two fellow detectives, Bobby Price and Jake Esteban, are ambushed during an undercover operation. Bobby is killed, while Jake is critically wounded, leaving Crockett and Tubbs determined to find those responsible.

Their investigation introduces one of Miami Vice’s most memorable recurring characters: Nugart Neville “Noogie” Lamont (Charlie Barnett).

Noogie is a fast-talking, streetwise hustler who claims to have connections to Desmond Maxwell, a key figure in the Jamaican drug operation. Although his information initially proves unreliable, Crockett and Tubbs discover that Noogie and Maxwell previously served time together.

Realizing he may be their best opportunity to reach the gang, the detectives recruit Noogie to help arrange an undercover drug deal.

Naturally, working with the Noogman proves anything but straightforward.

Between his outrageous personality, questionable reliability, and constant attempts to talk his way out of trouble, Noogie brings an entirely different energy to the investigation.

Meanwhile, Crockett faces another painful development in his personal life. His estranged wife, Caroline, serves him with divorce papers and reveals plans to move to Atlanta with their son, Billy.

For Sonny, the prospect of being separated from his son adds another emotional burden to an already dangerous job.

Back on the case, the detectives uncover evidence suggesting that the police have arrested the wrong suspect in connection with the shootings. A crucial clue involving a red Cadillac Eldorado helps Crockett and Tubbs realize that the real killers remain at large.

The investigation eventually leads to an undercover drug transaction at Noogie’s apartment.

But the situation quickly becomes dangerous when Maxwell’s men arrive and hold Noogie at gunpoint.

Crockett and Tubbs devise a plan to infiltrate the apartment and rescue their informant. With Tubbs concealed in the trunk of Sonny’s Ferrari Daytona Spyder, the detectives manage to overpower one of the gunmen and gain the advantage.

A SWAT-assisted raid follows, resulting in a violent shootout that brings the criminal operation to an end.

Noogie is wounded during the confrontation but survives.

The episode closes on a lighter note as Crockett and Tubbs encounter Noogie outside the hospital. The detectives offer him a box of candy as thanks for his assistance, but after everything he’s endured, Noogie isn’t particularly impressed.

Meanwhile, Jake is recovering from his injuries, providing some welcome relief after the tragedy that began the investigation.

“Cool Runnin’” delivers an entertaining balance of action, tragedy, and humor.

Charlie Barnett’s introduction as Noogie gives the series one of its most colorful personalities, while the murder of Bobby Price and Crockett’s ongoing family difficulties reinforce the darker realities beneath Miami’s glamorous exterior.

The episode’s reggae-influenced soundtrack, colorful Miami locations, and the unmistakable chemistry between Crockett and Tubbs continue building the identity of a series that was only beginning to find its rhythm.

Three episodes in, and Miami Vice is already firing on all cylinders, pal.

What did you think of Noogie’s debut? Did Charlie Barnett steal the episode, or was the action-packed investigation the real highlight?

See you out there, pal.  👇

text:
Mr.Sadanand Dhume wonders how I could use such disrespectful language to offend a senior Indian diplomat. He claims that Mr. Bai is utterly arrogant and impolite. Am I arrogant? No, not in the slightest. The truly arrogant one here is Mr. @VGokhale59  .

If you take the time to scroll through my posts on X or Zhihu, you will discover that I am perfectly capable of engaging in amicable discourse with anyone—provided their attitude toward me is equally respectful. When others launch attacks against me, I see no reason to adopt a hypocritical façade of magnanimity or tolerance; I hit back. If you notice that I leave certain malicious commentators unanswered, it is simply because I deem them unworthy of a response. This is precisely how the modern Chinese youth operates. To me, Mr. Gokhale’s response was unequivocally hostile.

As a seasoned former diplomat posted in China, Mr. Gokhale should know better: Chinese individuals express their personal viewpoints freely and easily across global platforms like X, Facebook, and Reddit. Yet, Mr. Gokhale reduced me to a mere cog in the CCP’s propaganda machine, dismissing me as part of a orchestrated international effort to fabricate a negative image of India—or, as many blithely put it, a "wumao." Descartes famously declared, “I think, therefore I am.” Free and independent thought is not something to be trampled upon, particularly when it comes to objective researchers. His attempt to distort my personal agency is not merely an act of genuine arrogance; it is a calculated humiliation.

Of course, there is another plausible explanation: despite having served as a diplomat in Beijing and speaking fluent Mandarin, Mr. Gokhale possesses surprisingly little genuine understanding of China. I do not offer this seemingly provocative conclusion lightly; it is backed by concrete evidence.

On May 27, 2026, Mr. Gokhale was interviewed by Mr. Shekhar Gupta on ThePrint. After watching it in its entirety, I was left thoroughly baffled. His observations regarding China made it hard to believe he is an authentic "China expert"—or rather, it reconfirmed my suspicion that the caliber of so-called "China hands" in India is strikingly substandard.

His core thesis was this: Beijing’s strategic encirclement and border leverage against New Delhi since 2013 stem from the fact that India’s democratic ideology poses an existential threat to China, compelling Beijing to contain and counterbalance India.

Mr. Gokhale’s logic is a rehash of a cliché popular two decades ago. Back then, a common narrative held that while China was outpacing India in raw growth, India harbored far greater long-term potential. If China was the hare, India was the tortoise—slower, perhaps, but endowed with far greater endurance.

The underlying premise of this argument was that China, under authoritarian and totalitarian rule, was plagued by widespread public discontent. Rapid economic expansion allegedly exacerbated wealth inequality and societal grievances, while state-owned enterprises choked out private enterprise, alienating economic elites. It was argued that these discontents would blame the system, yearn for liberal democracy, and ultimately mount a severe challenge to the regime, plunging China into intense political turmoil that would drag down its economy.

By contrast, India’s democratic framework was deemed superior and inherently more resilient. India simply needed to exercise patience and bide its time, and China’s economic dominance would unravel on its own. At that point, the Chinese populace would recognize the superiority of India’s democracy and turn further against rule at home. Hence, according to Mr. Gokhale, India presents an ideological threat to China, prompting Beijing’s geopolitical blockade in a desperate attempt to neutralize it.

Following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 and the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, "China collapse" theories gained tremendous traction, naturally fueling the absurd belief that India would eventually leapfrog China.

This mindset was epitomized in a famous essay by the Chinese-American scholar Yasheng Huang. In 2003, Professor Huang published an article titled "Can India Overtake China?" He argued that China’s state-owned sector was excessively bloated, holding a monopolistic grip on the market that stifled private enterprise and suppressed entrepreneurship. Furthermore, he claimed China’s growth was overly reliant on FDI, leaving it vulnerable to global economic shocks. India, conversely, boasted a more mature financial system, a healthier democratic framework, and political stability, granting it vastly superior long-term potential. Designed to cater to Western narratives of a "collapsing China" and a "rising India," the essay went viral, retaining its momentum for years.

Yet history proved Professor Huang fundamentally wrong. By 2026, Professor Huang published a follow-up essay titled "Twenty Years Later, Where Did My Predictions on China and India Go Wrong?" In it, he candidly admitted his past misjudgments and offered a deep self-examination. His core takeaway was simple: if the Chinese economy was a vehicle speeding along a cliff edge, he had failed to anticipate that the driver would steer away from danger in time.

This is precisely why I harbor deep skepticism toward Mr. Gokhale’s credentials as a "China hand." Furthermore, this view is hardly mine alone; numerous Chinese citizens and scholars thoroughly question Mr. Gokhale’s far-fetched theories.

It is not just Mr. Gokhale who lacks a real grasp of China; the same can be said for India’s External Affairs Minister, S. Jaishankar, another former ambassador to China. Since Mr. Jaishankar has not personally directed arrogant comments at me, I shall refrain from delving into personal critiques—lest I be accused of disrespecting him as well. Nevertheless, in September 2024, a scholar writing under the pen name Wang Daming published a sharp essay titled "The 'Jaishankar Problem' in Indian Diplomacy." The central premise was that the hostile and antagonistic posture toward China engineered by Jaishankar himself is the true culprit behind the freeze in Sino-Indian relations. For instance, Mr. Jaishankar has repeatedly asserted in public that the world faces a global "China problem," and that India's version of this problem is uniquely acute—involving not just border disputes, but deeper strategic rivalry—thereby framing India’s restrictive and defensive measures as mere "prudence."

To my knowledge, there is no public scholar in China named Wang Daming; it is a pseudonym. Unencumbered by a public identity, the author wrote with blunt, unapologetic candor. One passage from the article is particularly telling:

In India, there are many "China experts" like Jaishankar. Merely because their past assignments involved China or East Asia, they are anointed at home as definitive authorities on Chinese affairs. In reality, they understand neither China nor even India’s own fundamental national conditions and strategic interests; they possess little more than the ideological biases of the Indian elite. When Jaishankar claims that the international community faces a "China problem" and that China is a "country that operates in a fundamentally different way," he overlooks a key reality: many nations believe the "India problem" is the true predicament, viewing India as the state that operates on an anomaly—how else to explain why it is so notoriously difficult to deal with? When he argues that banning Chinese telecom technology is a national security necessity, one must ask: is American technology genuinely any safer? To date, we have never witnessed a "Huawei-gate" scandal, yet the world knows all too well the reality of "Prism-gate" exposed by Edward Snowden.

The Chinese public is rigorous and clear-minded. People do not blindly swallow the spin of self-proclaimed experts; they insist on observing and thinking for themselves. In my view, the general public in China possesses one of the highest levels of global literacy in the world. Benefiting from widespread, high-quality education and lifelong learning habits, combined with the instantaneous flow of internet information, everyday Chinese citizens can digest global news at home and arrive at sound, accurate conclusions. Indeed, the international insights offered by many independent Chinese content creators far surpass those of so-called "internationally renowned experts."

Mr. Gokhale approaches me with a patronizing, arrogant mindset, yet it is abundantly clear that his understanding of Chinese affairs is surface-level at best. Unfortunately, because the broader Indian public does not read Chinese, fails to comprehend Beijing's actions, and has long been fed a steady diet of negative coverage by domestic and Western media, the moment they encounter a former diplomat who speaks Mandarin, they reflexively label him a "China expert" and take his word as gospel. What Chinese observers find most bewildering is that when these Indian "China experts" are proven wrong, they invariably resort to silence rather than reflection. In contrast, scholars like Yasheng Huang undertake rigorous self-examination, exemplifying the classical Chinese ideal: "To know what you know and acknowledge what you do not know—that is true wisdom." Naturally, such intellectual honesty commands genuine respect.

If you are truly interested, you are more than welcome to visit China and observe it firsthand, rather than viewing it through the warped lens of malicious media. If travel funds are tight, you can simply hop onto YouTube travel channels and watch unfiltered videos filmed and narrated by vloggers from the US, the UK, Germany, India, Vietnam, Spain, Brazil, and beyond. That alone will give you a grounded, baseline impression—saving you from being misled by these official monopolists of knowledge.

text:
I am Chinese, and of course I speak from a Chinese perspective—what is there to reproach me for? Are Indian researchers supposed to interpret the border issue from a Chinese perspective? Moreover, even if I made a neutral and objective statement, would Indians believe it? You would still say I am not neutral or objective. As long as I am Chinese, Indians will never believe me.

Take Neville Maxwell of Australia—his research was neutral and objective enough, was it not? He worked as a journalist in Delhi for several years. He was once pro-India and unfriendly toward China, but when his India’s China War was published, India banned it. Why? Because the historical facts it described were regarded by the Indian government as anti-India. Indians may say within India that the war with China was Nehru’s fault, or the product of Kaul’s arrogance, and so on—but in external propaganda, it must always be China’s fault. That is no longer serious research.

I have carefully studied the Sino-Indian border dispute of 1962, including primary sources from both China and India, and I have tried to conduct my research from as neutral and objective a standpoint as possible. My research is more thorough than Maxwell’s, because I have access to abundant Chinese-language materials, yet my conclusions are almost identical to his. By both reason and justice, the party responsible for the 1962 war—and the greatest obstacle to resolving the current border situation—is India.

India’s current China studies are very poor. The core reason is the lack of Chinese perspectives and sources, which leads to interpretations of China that are almost entirely wrong, even laughable. If Indians wish to learn from historical experience, the right approach is to engage seriously with Chinese people, to discover the truths and facts that India failed to notice at the time, and thereby avoid repeating such a tragedy—not to treat an excellent Chinese scholar of India with a condescending sense of superiority.

Saying this will certainly be hard for many Indians to accept. OK, I understand the pain of Indians—who does not want their country to stand on the moral high ground? If you wish to refute me, then please present your research.

text:
A wealthy man offered a young woman $500,000 for her father's old house. She refused—and everyone thought she was crazy.
When 24-year-old Rachel inherited her father's small wooden house in Tennessee, her relatives couldn't understand why she wanted to keep it.
The roof leaked. The paint was peeling. The furniture was older than she was.
Then a real estate investor made her an offer.
“Half a million dollars,” he said. “You could buy a beautiful new home with that money.”
Rachel shook her head.
“No, thank you.”
Her relatives were furious.
“Your father is gone! That house is falling apart. Why are you throwing away your future?”
Rachel said nothing.
A week later, the investor returned with an even bigger offer.
She refused again.
Finally, he asked, “What could possibly make this house worth more to you than all that money?”
Rachel walked him to a small bedroom at the back of the house.
Inside was an old wooden desk covered in scratches. On the wall hung a photograph of her father holding her as a baby.
“When my mother died, I was only six,” she explained. “My dad worked as a mechanic during the day and cleaned offices at night to raise me.”
She opened a drawer and pulled out dozens of handwritten notes.
Whenever her father couldn't afford a birthday present, he wrote her a letter instead.
